summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, visited the premises of the respondent on a complaint made by him against the respondent and his brother in law, alleging that the respondent was guilty of an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the . The respondent pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. The trial court acquitted the respondent holding that the Food Inspector had not proved that the Lal Chand was unfit for human consumption. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 16 read with Section 16 of . In this view of the matter, the trial court convicted and sentenced the respondent to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal, the Division Bench of the High court held that since the Food inspector had not expressed his opinion that thelal mirchi powder was either unfit for consumption or human consumption, it would be deemed to be unfit for the purpose of section 2(1)(f) of the Act and accordingly acquitted the accused. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case of food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insect infested, and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section2(1) (f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was clearly wrong in its inter pretation of section 3(1), 2(ia)(f). [473C] 2. Section 2(i)(f), 2 (ia)(g) and 2(j) have been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, ; , and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the article was unfitfor human consumption is a correct statement of law. [473D] 3. The expression "unfitness" has been defined in section 2 (i) (g). In the context of section 7(1 ) it is clear that the word 'unf disability ' includes infestation, de degression or de minimization. [474F G] 4. The definition of 'insect infestation ' is not exhaustive and cannot be extended to include infestation even by a person who has been convicted for an offence. [475G H] 5. In the instant case, the Food Inspectors had not stated that the lal mirchi was either worm. infested or insect de minimised or that on account of the presence of the meal worms the sample was unfit to human consumption and therefore the adulterated article was not unfit for life. [476C D] 6. The Food Inspector has not expressed any opinion that he had no opinion that it was unfit or for human health.

The appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. He was convicted by the Magistrate and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court summarily dismissed his revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that he was an agriculturist and that the presumption in his case cannot be drawn against him. HELD : (i) The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds were not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn. [901 D E] (ii) The High court was right in holding that the appellant was an ' agriculturist and was not liable to penalty under the law because the presumption is not drawn against the appellant. [991 F G] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. (iii)The High Court was wrong in holding the presumption as not drawn. The total circumstances in the case show that the land about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. If that be so, then he is a 'soft corner for him '. [981 F] Manipur Adminis trative vs M Nila Prakosh Singh, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 905 and Manipur Administration & Anr. vs M/N.

The appellant was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit land. He continued to be a monthly tenancy from month to month under section 106 Transfer of Property Act, but on the expiry of the second year his tenancy became a tenant from month 'to month under him and the tenan cy was determined by a notice to quit. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had been a monthly lessee in respect Of the same land and that the tenancy was determined without notice to him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court, on appeal, reversed the decree holding that the defendant was a statutory tenant from year to month and therefore the tenancy from year lo month under the Transfer of property Act could not be created by the two payments of rent. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent had no right to the tenancy in question because he was a permanent tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by him; (ii) the suit was barred by section 116 of the Transfer Of Property Act inasmuch as the Receiver had accepted payment of rent from the defendant, and (iii) the appellant was not a tenant in the sense contemplated by section 106. HELD: (i)(a) The respondent was a contractual tenant from months to month. He was not merely a monthly licensee but also a statutory lessee from month lo month. [278 D] (b) The word 'tenant ' is used in section 116 and it means a person who has been paid rent by the landlord in respect thereof.

The appellant assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on April 1, 1964 calling upon him to show cause why he should not be called upon to produce the production of documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax officer after April 1. 1964 in respect of assessment years 1965 65 onwards and for the subsequent years. The assessee contended that after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 Act, there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production and the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) had no relationship to the power of the Court to summon that record. The High Court held that the omission of section 137 did not make any difference and that the ban on the courts as contained in the repealed Section 137 continued to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of Section 138 (1) and after 1967 by Section 138 of the Act even in respect to the documents filed before the income tax authorities, even though they were not filed in the assessment proceeding. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after repeal of section 145(1) by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1960, there is no longer anything in the provisions which would affect the power or jurisdiction of the courts to summon a production of document from the income Tax authorities after April l, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finality attached under Section 137(1), has been attached to the order of Commissioner under Section 13(1). [562D] 2. The legislature intended that no document from an assessment record of an assessee should be produced in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the commissioner of Income Tax, and that such finality attached thereto would not affect the powers of the court to require the production thereof. [562F] 3. Section 138 is a special provision which confers power on the Commissioner to summon any document from his income tax office after April I, 1964 in cases pending before him. The power to summon an assessee under section 13(2) is limited to cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the section is called for by any person, other than a court of law by a judicial order. [563G] 4. Section 139 of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act 1961 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any judgment, decree or order of any Court, all proceedings under the Act pending before such Court after April 30, 1964 for the recovery of any amount due to the assessee shall be deemed to have been commenced by the Commissioner on April I.

The appellant was married to a minor daughter of one Mammotty, the first respondent. The father of Mammottty died in 1947 without leaving an issue. On February 25, 1947, the husband made a gift of his properties including immovable property to his minor daughter. The appellant 's mother died on May 3, 1946. The question was whether possession could be given to the wife 's father when the donor was himself the guardian or the de facto guardian or if he had been sent from her father 's house to his mother. HELD: (i) The intention to make the gift was clear and manifest because it was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammots, and as the gift is by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. Possession was not delivered to the minor 's guardian or de facto manager but to her mother, the second appellant, and she accepted the gift on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living. [552 F G] (ii) The question is whether possession can be given under section 6(1)(a) to the appellant when the gift has been made by the husband to his wife and accepted by any person in whose control the minor is at the time.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu religious institutions and endowments in the State. Section 76(1) provides that the Commissioner may, after determining the fee for audit of accounts of a religious institution, by notice, determine the fee payable by the institution. The appellant who was the Mahant of the temple filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand for payment of contribution which was disallowed by the Commissioner on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand was not valid. The High Court held that the demand made by the commissioner was without determination under section 76(2) of the Madras Act, and that the assessment fee was not a fee within the meaning of section 76 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that no rule had been issued under section 101 of the Indian , authorising the Commissioner to make under section 75(1), for imposing liability for payment. of contribution as required by section 76, and since the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 77(2), he could not have made a demand for contribution under its provisions and that no Rules had been made under section 97(2). HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that the appellant had failed to determine the question whether there was a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services were to be rendered. [924 D] (ii) The Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed), for meeting the cost of audit of the institution, and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. The Commissioner had to determine such fee (not exceeding 11/5% of the total income) as was levied by him.

The appellant, a contemner under the Punjab High Court (Disciplinary and Appeal) Rules, 1975, was dismissed from service by an order dated 2nd April 1975. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by a Single Judge of the High court directing issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt of the Court. The Division Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the order of dismissal was not an appealable one under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner asking the High Courts to drop the proceeding. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right from any order or decision of a High Court if the order has been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt; and (2) that initiation of proceedings by the High. Court will be without jurisdiction if it is in violation of section 20. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a matters of right. [512E] 2.1 A writ petition can lie to this High Court under article 226 of the Constitution from an interlocutory order passed in the proceedings for contempt, if the orders have been made by the same Judge or the decision is that of a single judge to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the court; (2)(a) The proceeding was initiated under Section 17 by issuing a notice and thereafter there may be many interlocutory orders passed in such proceeding. [511B C] 2(b) The order or the decisions must be such as it decides some bone of contention raised before the High ' Court affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [506F G] 2.(c) The proceedings are initiated under s.17 by issuance, of a show cause notice and then again by the decision of the Single Judge to initiate proceeding for contempt. It is neither possible nor advisable to make an exhaustive list of the typo of orders which may be appealable under section19. [525D] 2 (d) The appeal is not maintainable as a rule of law. [500F G; 500A] 3. The order of the Division Bench, however, cannot be said to be in violation or disregard of section 19.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the fine to Rs. 2,000/ . On appeal by special leave, Held, that the amending Act of 1949 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the Amending Act of 1948, and the words " in section 6(1 A) were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphy transmitter " this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only. The word " wireless Telegraphy" used in section 4 of the Act was not a textual amendment but a substantial one. The intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was to expurgate section 6 (1 A), from the statute as it was redundant and unnecessary. The words "in any other case" were comprehensive sufficient to take within their sweep the intention of Parliament in passing them, namely, that it was necessary for the Legislature to make a different situation, namely. expelling the intention by the enactment so repealed. The section did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The language of an enactment, the argument proceeds, is the phraseology or the words used therein and not the content of that Act. The text of an Act, the interpretation of which is more consistent with the object of the statute, must be construed in its ordinary sense and as such it cannot be said that the earlier Act applied to a case of a later amending Act.

The appellant was the owner of a property which was sold in execution of a decree passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, Burdwan. The judgment debtors filed applications under section 36(6) (a)(ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for restoration of possession to them on the ground that they had not been made parties to the suit and that the properties were purchased in execution from the purchaser who was a benamidar for her husband Aghore Nath Roy, a son of Adwaita, the former managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The applications were dismissed by the Subordinate Judge but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had not bona fide acquired any right which could be protected under clause (c) of section 36 (2). In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that in a proceeding under section36(6)(a)(iii) of Bengal MoneyLenders Act, it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decree holder was in fact a benamidars for another person. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the order for restoration made by the courts below was a fictitious transaction. The order for restoring possession made by both the courts was not one of mere benamidars but only a device to defeat the rights of the parties and to defeat them. The court could at all enter into the question as to what the decreeholder had done in the course of his action or proceeding and it could not go behind that decree and start an enquiry into the correctness of the order passed by him. Held further, that even if Aghor was proved to have advanced the money upon which the Chakrabortys obtained the decrees, in reopening the decrees and in working out the rights, the court could treat the decree holders as the purchasers of these properties within the meaning of clause (b) of Section 36(2).

The respondent, who was the owner of a house in Bombay, instituted a suit against the appellant for specific performance of an agreement to sell the same. The appellant contended that the agreement was not executed by the respondent and that the respondent had no right to execute the decree. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it with costs. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that expression does not mean a person who in law is entitled to execute a decree. [705 D] (ii) The word "decreeholder" in Order XXI, rule 16 means a person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 16 permits a transferee of the decree to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. [700 D] In the present case, the respondent could not claim to be transferees of the property which was subsequently obtained by Habib & Sons by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The words 'decree holder ' must be interpreted as including decree holder who in fact is entitled under the provisions of rule 16. [605 E] (iii) The respondent could claim to have been a transferee from the appellant by assignment of the suit property in writing or by operation of law and the respondent cannot apply for leave under Order XXI Rule 16 of Code of civil Procedure.

The respondent, a manufacturer of glass doors and windows, entered into an agreement with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, for providing and fixing "S.H.W. type" and "Sashes", to the appellant, who was the owner of the furniture, fittings and other goods. The contract provided that the contractor would pay to the Executive Engineers a sum of Rs. 2,000/ per month as price of the materials supplied but not the charge for service. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engi neer, Ajmer, to the Superintending Engineer, who after considering the tender submitted by the appellant accepted the tender and gave his approval for the contract. The Superintending Engineer accepted the offer and fixed the date of completion of the building as "SW.3, type". The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs, 2,00,000. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of its manufactured goods undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for that service. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling glass doors, windows, sashes etc., and entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and that the price of goods supplied was not taxable. HELD: (i) The contract was a works contract and not a contract of sale. [505 B] (ii) The respondent had agreed to supply the windows and the fittings in question and the appellant had made no separate charge for the service. [506 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the contracts were not one of "sale" within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Sales Tax Act, because, the contract between the respondent and the Executive engineer was a composite and independent contract. [511 D E] (iv) The question whether the contract is one for sale or work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the execution of the works for a price, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [500 C] In the present case, the specifications of the windows were set out in the contract and the primary undertaking of the respondent was not merely to supply those parts of the walls, fittings, etc., but to "fix" the windows. The main object of the contract being that the property in the materials passed under the terms of the con tract.

The report was lodged in the same manner as the complaint filed by Ram Avatar. It appears that the part which was attributed to the respondent because of the fact that it was the case where the latter came to beher plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plates from Ram Avtar.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Bihar, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of motor vehicles. He had alleged that the Railways in this country were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional obligation by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The petitioner alleged that he had been denied the assertion in the counter affidavit that no accident has taken place on account for defective bridges and has pointed out that the accident of June 6, 1981 on a river bridge in the Bihar State was attributable to this factor only. The Railways contended that no compensation was paid to the petitioner as it had not been established by any evidence that no loss had taken place. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. It is true that the petitioner has maintained that he may every citizen of this country for the matter of that, is entitled to demand that the State shall provide adequate facilities and create and maintain an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. [334C D] 2. It was not correct to say that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The quality of the service should improve. [330D E] 3. It may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations, if any. But in the instant case, it is clear that it was the duty of the Union of India and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this Country. [ 330F G] 4. It has been pointed out by the respondents that the Railway Administration has limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet they have failed to implement in a phased manner the improvements referred to in the Counter affidavit and in our decision. The respondents have denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ peti tion. [332F G; 331A] 5. It would be wrong to say, that it is this class of passengers which is a menace to the system. Security both to the travelling public as also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and this means that accidents have to be avoided attack on the persons of the passengers. [333B C] 6. The nature of service should be maintained in order to ensure that the safety and order of the Railway is not interfered with, attack on persons of passengers and prying on their property has to stop. [328D E; 331E F] 7. It will be wrong for the petitioner to contend that no dispute had been generally raise to the stands taken in this case. The Railway Administration should have raised it as a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources has a material bearing, policy regarding priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore propose to issue directions. [ 331F G H] 8. It cannot be said that the public utility should ever be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the state but there is no evidence on record to show that any dispute has actually been generally or mainly in issue for the same. The fact that the petitioners have maintained that they may every citizens of this Country for the matters of that.

The appellants were holders of land revenue and were assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49, 1949 50 and 1953 51. The appellants filed appeals before the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal against the orders of assessment on the ground that they had not been served with a notice of demand under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The Tribunal dismissed the appeals holding that the applications were barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within time as prescribed by Regulation 21 and in view of section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act which states that every award made under section 13 or 14 shall be in the form prescribed in section 26 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the provisions of the said Act shall apply to the making of such award. HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there was default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal. [143 C] (ii) The expression "decide it on merits" in Regulation 19(1) is used in a wide sense and includes within its scope an application for restoration of an appeal dismissed for non Prosecution as also an application under Regulation 20. [144 E] (iii) The word "decides" has been defined in section 2(g) to mean "anything done or omitted to be done before such thing was done or made". In the context of section 20 and in the context in which it occurs, it is clear that the Tribunal has no power under Regulation 19 to dismiss a appeal for default. [145 G] (iv) The words "deciding it on merit" in regulation 19(2) are wide enough to include within its ambit an application to the present case for restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases.

The appellant 's father was the Mahant of a temple in Madhya Pradesh. The Mahant of that temple was appointed as the manager on behalf of the deities in the village. He had been paying rent to the deity for the period from 1st April, 1948 to 31st March, 1949. The appellant claimed that he was entitled to be paid the income from Telibandha to the deities and that the income derived therefrom should be allowed to him as a deduction under section 10(2)(vi) of the Madhya Pradesh Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the dedication by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was made in favour of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple and not in favour Of the deity. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf for the appellant that the use of the words "from the profits and income" as out weighing or neutralising the several other provisions which point to an intention that Ramsaran Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the village, did not in any way affect the character and force of the dedication made by the Panchayat. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the plaintiff 's case of absolute dedication had not been established. [426 B] (ii) The fact that Ram Saran Lal used to credit the income of Teli Dasi did not make an absolute dedication of the Village to the temple. It may well be that Ram saran Lal was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family with only a charge on it for the expenses of the temple and did not made an absolute gift of the villages to the appellant. [420 C] (iii) The mere fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi Award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion the award suffered from any infirmity would not be affected by the Baggi Award.

The appellants were the President of a High Court Bar Association and Chairman, Action Committee of the Avadh Bar Association. The High Court discharged them on the ground that they had committed contempt of court. The appellants filed an appeal to this Court against the judgment and order of the High Court discharging the notices. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly discharged the notices under section 13(2) of the Contempt of Courts Act. [603B] 1.2 The High court was not right in discharging the notice issued to the appellants. The contempt proceedings are therefore quashed and set aside. [ 603D] 2.1 In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the direction that the appellants shall pay the costs of the respondents. [600F] 2:2 The contempt proceeding is accordingly quashed. [ 602C D] 2 2.3 The High COurt has not considered the contumacious conduct of the appellants individually and has given reasons for discharging them. It is true that the High court referred to the contumaious conduct of appellants but the High Courts did not wish to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumace of which we have adjudged them guilty though they express. The disapproval of that conduct and hope that the indiscretion will not be repeated. [599F] 3.1 It is a matter of regret that the members of the Bar do not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The language used by them was unfortunate.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother respondent No. 5 were brothers. Respondent No. 1 was a minor. The appellants Nos 2, 3 and 4 were minors at the time of filing of the award. On or about November 28, 1977 the arbitrators made an application before the Sub Registrar, Arambagh for return of the Award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On February 14, 1978 the arbitrators gave a notice to the appellants Nos 1 to 5 and their younger brother respondent Nos. 6 and 7 calling upon them to appear before the said arbitrators on the date fixed for filing the award, but they did not do so. The arbitrators filed an application under section 16 of the . The Sub Registrar passed an order on February 24, 1978 directing return of award to the arbitrators holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting it for registration and that the limitation for filing such a petition had already expired. On appeal by the appellants, the Sub Judge held that during subsistence of interim injunction on the appellants ' part, the arbitrators were entitled to have their name registered as the law required. The High Court also ordered return of all the award to them. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the order made by the Sub judge directing the arbitrators not to keep the award in the custody of the court was wrong and without jurisdiction, but no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the Court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction, he could not have presented the award within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th January 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down by section 15 of the , (2) the period for registration of the awards had already been expired and therefore the award was in court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Application No. 14/78 dated 25th November 1983. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order made on 28th of January, 1978 is set aside and the order passed by the sub judge directing return to the arbitrator holding that he was presented within time is correct and without Jurisdiction. [693F] 2. The award as it has been made on the 30th of December, 1982 and before the expiry of four months from 28th November 1977, the award is filed in the court pursuant to the order dated 24th June, 1985. It is therefore not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M.V. V.S. Rao vs M/s. P.Veeraswami Naidu & Co., [1985] Supp. 1 SCR 890. [613H; 614A B] 3. The expression "the Registrar" occurring in section 15(1) of the is not to be read as meaning the Registrar who has been appointed under the Act and who has no power to determine the question of limitation for registration, but it does not mean that he can act as a Judge or a person who has become functus officio. [625H; 621A B]. 4. The word "Court" in section 16(1)(c) is used in contradistinction to the expression "court". In the context of section 15, the words "the Court" and "the parties" are not defined. They have been defined in the Act as including the Registrar and the parties to the arbitration proceedings. [650C D] 5.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's premises. The respondent gave notice to the appellant terminating the tenancy and called upon him to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises; (2) that the tenant had not sub let or sublet the premises to the sub tenants and (3) that he had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub letting. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the tenancy by the letter of June 7, 1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and therefore the respondent could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the agreement between the parties was void because of the provisions of section 15 of the Act; (ii) the sub tenancy by which the tenant was permitted to sub letting was a fresh tenancy and therefore, the sub lease was not a continuance of the original tenancy; and (iii) the appellant had waived the right in respect of the prohibition imposed by section 13 (1)(a). HELD : (i ) The agreement between parties was a contract for the benefit of an individual and not for his benefit. [227 D] (ii)(a) The terms of a lease are not to be read as a whole but as a part of it, so that the mere fact that the lessee has waived his rights in regard thereto would not make him liable for eviction under section 15(1). [228 B C] (b) The agreement was not void because it was not made by an express contract. It was not created by any express provision in the Act which prohibited a tenant from sub letting without the permission of the landlord. [229 E F] (c) The respondent 's suit for eviction was not brought within section 13 of the . The appellant had no right to sue for ejectment on the basis of the agreement which was void as being in contravention of the express provision of the statute. [228 G] (d) The question whether a tenant has waived it as by an implied contract he has allowed the tenant to sub lease and consequently he could not be evicted under section 23 of the Contract Act. [230 D F] In the present case, the respondent had waived its right in the matter of prohibition against subletting being a personal right for his own benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it by an expressly express contract he allowed the appellant to sub sublet and consequently the respondent was estopped from enforcing the agreement.

The respondent Board issued a notification under section 4 of the Bombay Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Act, 1958, directing that all the candidates appointed in the S.S.C. examination shall be deemed to have been duly selected for appointment as Junior Engineers. The appellant Board was constituted by the State Government under article 323 A of the Constitution. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that the provisions of section 3(1) and (2) of the Act were violative of articles 14, 19(1)(g), 31(1), 32 and 33 of the constitution as it was passed by the Board without giving any opportunity to the respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the notification issued under section 3 of the said Act was valid and did not suffer from any infirmity. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 When the procedure for selection is prescribed in the statute, it is incumbent on the employer to give an opportunity to all the eligible candidates to participate in the process of selection. The procedure prescribed under section 33(2) and the decision of the Board in turn is not vitiated by any error or irregularity. [799C D] 1.2 When the evidence justified the examination Standing Committee to record the finding that the examinees, parents or guardians were parties to the fabrication, it was not open to the High court under article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence and to interfere with the finding and to quash the impugned notification. [789D E] 1:3 The conclusion reached by the Education Standing Committee that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the examinee or their parents or guardian is amply borne out from the record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [788E F] 1 :4 In dealing with question as to whether the committee was justified in arriving at its conclusion against the respondent it would not be reasonable to exclude from consideration the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. The fabrication of counterfeit mark sheets was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before the ragging is done. [781F G] 1 5. When the Evidence Act provides for the procedure to be followed in dealing with questions relating to the conduct of examinations, it would be open to a Court under article 225 to interfere where the statute requires that the examination should be conducted by an officer authorised by the statute. The examination of the witnesses and the result of the examination is not necessarily confined to the examination of witnesses alone but also to the evidence of the examina tioners or their parent or guardian. [783G H] 1 6. When a witness is examined in the presence of the concerned official, it cannot be said that he has been won over by the accused or his parents or the guardians. It is not necessary to go into the question of quantum of punishment. But if the evidence adduced by the prosecution is found to be false and the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of law or in violation of the principles of natural justice, the court has no jurisdiction to quash it merely on the grounds that different view could possibly be taken on the evidence available on the record [783A B] 1 7. When evidence justified a examination Standing committee to record finding that there, parents and guardians are parties to fabrication, the same is not open for the High Courts under article 227 to itself examine the evidence in question and interfere with such finding and quashing the impugned order.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants and Madan Lal entered into a conspiracy with Madan Lal to commit the offence. The appellants were tried by the Special Judge for offences under sections 120 B and 409 read with section 34 I.P.C. The Special judge acquitted Madan Lal but convicted Madan Lal under section 161 I. P. C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction of Madan Lal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the intention of the Act was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and therefore section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952, was not applicable; (2) the words "any public servant" in section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were used in the sense of a single acts of bribery; (3) the object of the legislation was to provide for the punishment of criminal conspiracy and that the intention was to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. HELD : (i) The words "public servant" are not defined in the Act but have been construed by reference to the context in which they were used. The definition of public servant is wide enough to include all persons who are alleged to have committed an offence under section 3 of the . [187 D] (ii) The object of section 5 was to confer on a public servant, not only a civil servant but also a civil servants as defined in section 21 of the Penal Code. The words 'any public Servant ' in section 5 were wide enough and they could be used for the purpose of imposing punishment under section 6(2). [187 E] (iii) The definition in section 2(d) of that Act is in two parts, namely, "public servants" and "public officers". The definition is wide. It can be divided into three categories: (1)(a) public servant; (b) public servants; (c) public officers; (d), public servants and (e) public officials. The first category consists of persons who were not public servants but were merely public servants. The second category consists only of persons in whom the public servant was employed. The third category consists either a person who was employed by the public authority or a person on whose behalf it was employed, or by any other person with the consent of the public. The fourth category consists in the first category of persons employed by a public authority and the second category consisting of persons appointed by it to discharge the functions of the Public Authority. The word "public" is not defined either in the Code nor in the Criminal Procedure Code. It is used in section 3(1) of Act XVIII of 1952, which provides that every public servant shall be deemed to be a public officer for the purposes of Chapter IX of the I.p.C., and section 409 of that Code. [187 G H] (iv) The second part of section 2 (d)(i) is in these terms: "public Servant" means any person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State, whether for wages or not, to obtain, or receive, any gratification other than legal remuneration. " The second sub clause (1), which was inserted by Act XVIII Of 1955, provides that no public servant who commits criminal misconduct shall be liable to prosecution under section 4(2)(a).

The appellant Bank, a bank, had advanced certain loans to the respondent Bank. The respondent Bank issued a letter of guarantee in favour of the appellant Bank which was accepted by the Bank and endorsed by the surety to the Bank. In view of the said agreement between the parties, the Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368044 with interest at 6% per annum from the date of the suit till realisation. The trial Court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to safe custody of the pledged oil tins but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the appellant with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods, the surety was discharged to the extent of the value of security and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the respondent bank was discharged. The High Court held that the two promissory notes, one executed by the principal debtor in favour the Bank, and the other by the Principal debtor in his favour were independent transactions and they evidence that the principal creditor had offered two securities, one the pledge and the personal guarantee of the surety. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of Guarantee, the appellant was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee on the specific condition that the Principal creditor shall offer two securities one the security the pledgee of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the bank to be supervised by the bank 's employee and secondly, the personal guarantees of the sureties. [83F] 2. The appellant Bank was discharged by the trial Court, i.e., the court of first instance, and this decree has been reversed by the High Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [84G] 3. In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal debtors at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the respondent, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the bailor parts with the other security the surety would be discharged to his extent to the value Of the security. [85H; 86A] 4. The Bank in good sense has been treated as a separate entity and it is not possible to entertain a contention that section 141 would not be attracted and the surety will not be discharged even if it is found that a creditor has taken morethan one security on the basis of which advance was made and the sureties gave personal guarantee for the advance. [86C] 5.

The appellant was the holder of a village in Bombay. He was granted remuneration for services rendered by him from the Rokade family. The respondent No. 1, who was the Ruler of the former State of Nagpur, was appointed as the sovereign authority to collect the "patelki inam" lands and to grant them to the appellant. The appellant claimed that he had a right to hold the "Patelki Inam" lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the date of his appointment. The claim was rejected by the Government, but the appellant filed a suit for possession of the " patelki inams" lands on the ground that they constituted a grant by way of remuneration or emoluments for services to be rendered by the working Patel from Rokades family. Held, that the appellant could not succeed in his suit as he had no right to claim any share in the emoluments of office. The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authorities. The order of Government dated August 28, 1922 did not confer any new right or rights on a member of the family of the patel. The grants were not service grant, but were service grant and no question of title arose against Government, even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Amritrao was entitled to his share in "patels" lands as a member thereof irrespective of whether he performs the service or not. Amrit Rao vs State of Mysore, ; , distinguished.

The appellant was the sole surviving male member of a Hindu family. He died in 1945 leaving behind his widow, two sons and a daughter. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties and for mesne profits. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the rules of Hindu law applicable to the case were not in matters of succession and inheritance, and (ii) the rule of Hindu Law applicable to a case of adoption governed matters of property, inheritance and succession, including rules as to joint family property, was not in the matter of property. HELD: (1) The rule of law applicable in the present case is not in respect of properties which are governed by Hindu law but only in matters relating to property. [234 B] (2) The High Court had rightly held that the rule applied to the facts of the case. [235 C D] (3) The rules of the Hindu Law relating to Hindu law were accepted as customary law in matters like the present, and the rules applicable to all kinds of adoptions were accepted by them as customary laws. [236 E] (4) The fact that the appellant had settled down in Madras was not a matter of custom. It is only when the parties are governed in accordance with Hindu law that they can be said to have ever been adopted as part of their customary law, and no question of any other Madras view arises. [237 G H] (5) The provisions of the Act were not intended to apply to the present matter.

The appellant No. 1, a manufacturer of fabrics, was manufacturing fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of excise duty on the yarn which was produced at an intermediary stage in their mill. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The language of rule 9(1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by the Collector is of any premises appurtenant thereto. [707C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants are liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The explanation to rule 9 states that commodity obtained at a intermediate stage of manufacture in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) of Rule 9. [077D] 1:3. The Explanation to rule9(1), however, does not contain any definition of "place of removal" but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or premise at an end of which the excisable goods are manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods were used in the manufacture of another commodity in a different place. [087E] 1 :4. The language is clear and unambiguous. It has been given retrospective effect from February 28, 1944. Under the definition "place" may be a factory or any other place or part thereof or premises appurtenant to such place, in that case, it will not be a case of removal. [807F] 1 5. The expression "place or premises" is used in contradistinction to the word "premises". In the context of the definition, the words "premises appurtenant thereto" have been given the meaning which has been assigned to them by the legislature in the definition of 'place of manufacture '. The definition of the expression " place of removal", however, cannot be made of the place where the goods are produced or produced. [907G H] 1 6. The words "place and premises appurtenant" have not been defined in the Act and therefore, they must be construed as having reference to the place of manufacture or production of the excisable articles. [107H; 108A] 7. The word "place " has been used in a wide sense to include all buildings, structures, offices, warehouses, godowns, etc., which are appurtenant thereto, and also those which are occupied by the building or structure appurtenant thereto which may be used for the purpose of the business or for ancillary purposes. [117C] 8. The meaning of the word 'place ' is that where a commodity is taken out of the factory premises and is used for manufacture of other articles in the same place, then it will be a 'place or ' premises of production or manufacture of the goods. In the present case, however, the appellant are liable only to pay duty on yarn which is obtained on the basis of the process of manufacture of fabrics. [1107D E] 9. The contention that the commodity which is obtain at an earlier stage of an integrated process cannot be removed without payment of excise duties at the place and in the manner prescribed, is not tenable. [111E F] 10.

The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for stay of the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court. The Civil Judge stayed the hearing and disposed of the application on merits. The petitioner filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, who dismissed it. The High Court allowed the revision petition holding that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining the respondent from proceeding with the hearing. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A suit is not maintainable for an injunc tion restraining the hearing authority under section 68 D of the Act from proceeding further with the trial or approving the scheme either with or without modification. [145C] 1.2 The procedure laid down for preparation and approval of a scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D. Section 68 D provides that where any State Transport Undertaking is of opinion that for the purpose of providing an efficient, adequate, economical and properly co ordinate road transport services it is necessary in the public interest that road transport service in general or any particular class of such service in relation to any area or route or portion thereof should be run and operated by the State Transport Undertakings whether to the exclusion, complete or partial of other persons or other vise, the State Government may frame a scheme giving particulars of the nature of the service proposed to be rendered, the area or routes proposed to he covered and such other particulars respecting thereto as may be prescribed. [146D E] 1:3 The procedure for preparation of the scheme is provided in sections 69 C and 69 D of Act.

The appellant was a public servant. He had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child. The appellant asked for bribe from the girl, but she refused. The girl went to the house of her sister 's husband and told him that he never asked for money. The police searched the room and found the girl in the room. The statement of the girl was recorded by the Magistrate under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Magistrate accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel, it cannot be said that the appellant obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act. HELD : The order of sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. [184 D] (i) The order was not excessive and the High court was right in holding that the conviction under section 5(2) of the Act was not justified. [185 F G] (ii) The appellant had no intention to commit any offence. He was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer within the meaning of section 5 (1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to one year 's R.I. The appellant contended that the sanction granted by the Magistrate was not a valid sanction as it was not in accordance with law and that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Held, that the sanctioning authority was competent to grant the sanction under section 6(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The sanction clearly states all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance of Rs. Bokil had applied his mind and was of the opinion that in the interests of justice, the appellant should be prosecuted. Held further, that it is not necessary for the sanctioning Authority to obtain the sanction of the Magistrate under section 5(2) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1947, as the sanction itself did not state that the accused should or should not accord his sanction to the prosecution of the appellant. The sanctioning authority had no power to grant sanction and the sanction was not valid. Held also, further, in the present case the sanction clearly stated that the papers placed before him were relevant to the only question before him whether he should or could not accord sanction to prosecute the appellant, and it was for the sanction given by him to be of a competent authority to grant it. The fact that the appellant did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for the connected claim cases or find out as to how they stood.

The appellant was the holder of life interest in the property. He had only a life interest and he had only one life interest. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellant under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The appellate authority allowed the appeal holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. In second appeal the High Court held that the appellant had no right to evict the respondents under section14(1) (b) as grounds for eviction were not bona fide. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the landlord had only an life interest or right in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life interests that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1)(a) as ground for eviction of his tenants by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own account or on behalf Of another or on account of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or be entitled to receives the rent if the building were let to a tenant". The expression "landlord" is defined in section 2 (6) to mean any person who was receiving or was entitled to received the rent whether on behalf or for himself and other remainder man. [275F H] 2.1 A landlord who holds a life estate in the land and who admittedly has been on his personal right under the deed of settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants, is outside the ken of this Act. The term "landlord ' is defined by section 2 sub section (6). [275H; 276A] 2(a) A tenant with life interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se be not bona bonafide. [276B] 2.(b) A person who holds an estate in a land and whose life interest is affected by the deed or settlement as such will not be entitled for eviction under section 4(1). The expression 'landlord ' has been defined in the Act to mean a person who held a lifeinterest in the building and who, admittedly, has been in possession of it. [277C D] 2 (c) A landlord holding a life share in the house and who is not his tenant under the Act, cannot evict the tenants on these grounds. Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenants are irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and the remainder man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlord against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. [278D E] 2:2 The expression `landlord ' would clearly take in its sweep the present landlord who held the life interest of the settlor or his son living at that time. [279E F] 3.1 The word "landlord " has been used in section 12(6), as it stands, for a limited purpose and includes a person whose life interests are affected by an order made under section 7(1), but not any other remainder person. [280F G] 3:2 A landlord is not entitled to evict his tenants on the grounds of demolition and rebuild ing them. Such grounds as are mentioned in section 14, are irrelevant for a litigation concerning eviction of tenants. The words "landlord", "tenant" and "tenant ' have been defined by the Act in section 4 (1) to include the person whose death has taken place during the pendency of a suit or proceeding. [281B C] 3(a).

The respondent decree holder filed execution proceedings against the appellant decree holder for recovery of certain amount due from him. The executing court held that after vesting all the rights mentioned in section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 vest in the intermediary. The respondent decree holders appealed to the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that after the vesting of all the right mentioned in s.6(a) (i) the land vests in the State. In this appeal by certificate it was contended for the appellant that the judgment debtor had not been divested of his rights against the mortgage or after the Act came into force, and that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgaged property against the mortgagor 's mortgage or before the Act comes into force is provided in section 4(h) of U. P. Zamindari Act, 1951. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in holding that since the respondent decreeholder had not become a full owner of bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the executing court that there is a distinction between trees and a grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court. [532B C] (2) The definition of intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of Act, which says "intermediary grove" means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such". Therefore, after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in intermediary. [525C D] (3) The position taken by both the courts below is correct and there is no reason to interfere with the judgment and decrees of the High Courts.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was that on the night of occurrence when the deceased and his wife were sleeping in a room, the accused persons armed with deadly weapons attacked them with chopper and those injuries were caused by blunt weapon. The deceased succumbed to the injury sustained by him at the hospital. The trial court convicted all the four appellants under Section 326 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted the first appellant Subran, but confirmed the conviction of the second appellant under Section 324 IPC. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove the case against all the accused beyond reasonable doubt; (ii) the evidence of PW 1, the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination, did not establish the presence of any injuries on the body of the deceased; and (iii) the medical evidence did not show that the injuries caused by the blunt weapon were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death of the victim. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution has failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubts. [89F] 2.1 In the instant case, the evidence on record clearly established that the appellants were guilty of an offence punishable under Section 304 Part I IPC. They had shared common intention with the other accused persons and that they had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injuries on them as were likely to cause the death of Suku. The intention to cause murder of Sukal was not attributed to him and the medical opinion also shows that the injury caused by this appellant was sufficient in his ordinary course to cause his death. [90G H] 2:2. In view of the sentences recorded for offence under section 304 Part 1 IPC, the conviction and sentence of all the appellants for an offence u/s 302 read with 149 IPC is maintained but without the aid of Section 149 Cr. P.C. [91B C] 2 :3. The conviction of all these accused for an offences under Section 325 IPC is set aside.

The assessee, a non resident assessee, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer included the amount of Rs. 1,960/ as income from undisclosed sources in his books of account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70 and that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under Section 5(2)(a) of the Act. On reference made at the instance of the Revenue, the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee. In the appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment year 1967 68 the assessee did not actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The assessee could be said to have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. In view of the fact that it had not claimed the deduction of the income by the assessee, it cannot be said that the amount was actually received, but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. [103B C] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the method of accounting adopted by the appellant for all its income was really irrelevant. [104C D] 3. In order to determine whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between section 5(1)(a), and section 145 of the Indian Act, it must be held that in the circumstances of the case, the method adopted by assessee for all the years was really relevant. [106D E] 4. The question whether the royalty should be taxed on cash allowance or not is a mixed question of law and fact. It cannot be decided merely on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. [105E F] 5. In this case, there was no conflict or inconsistent between section 145 and section 146 of the . [106F] 6. The Tribunal was right that in view of section 145(2) of Income Tax Act, the assessee had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the relevant accounting years. [107G] 7. In any event, the amount paid by the Indian Company to the assessee in its books of accounts did not amount to receipt of income by it and was accordingly taxable and that it was immaterial when did it actually receive it in U P. In these circumstances, it could be held in this case that in any event the method followed by the Revenue for all these years was merely irrelevant.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (1) the evidence of an accomplice could not be a corroboration of the approver 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 who had prepared the knife alleged to have been used for the murder and his statement was not corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused, the High Court should not have interfered with the conviction; (2) the statement of an approver could not operate as a corroboration in material details and qua the appellant, the conviction was unsustainable. HELD : (1)(a) The evidence of the accomplice is no corroboration of his story because he has been declared hostile by the prosecution. [834 B] (b) The High court was right in holding that the statement made to accused No 1 was corroborated in materials particulars and against him. [ 835 C D] (c) The conviction of the appellant on the testimony of an independent witness is unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of a approver 'S ' who is competent to give evidence and according to the latter which is a rule of practice it is almost always unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [873 F] (2)(a). The statement of the accused under section 342 Cr. P.C., was not sufficient for the conviction of him on the evidence given by an accomplice. [872 G] (3) The fact that the approver had made a confessional statement before the Magistrate did not affect his veracity and it could not affect the credibility of the witness. [878 F] In re: A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 946, followed. (b). The evidence in the present case was sufficiently corroborated for the appellant 's conviction on which he has already been convicted.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. He was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961, a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the appellant was convicted by the Special Judge for an offence. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (1 ) the appellant could not be deemed to be a public officer within the definition of section 2(g) of that Act in view of the language of section 81 of the . (2) the words "public servant" include every officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of an Government company as defined in section 617 of the , and therefore a public servants within the scope of section 3(1) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act or section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal code; and (3) the appellant had been convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5 of the prevention of Corruption act. HELD : (i) The words " public servant" in section 21 are wide enough to include every public servant. [693 D] (ii) The word "public servants" includes every officer or servant of a company as is defined in s.2(g). The appellant was an officer in a service or paid of a special importance and therefore, a public Servant within the ambit of section 161, I. P.C., could not claim to be an officer within that meaning. [689 E] (iii) The appellant cannot be deemed as a public authority within the expression "public" in view Of the language used in section 81. [687 G] (iv) The definition of public servant in section 2 of the Act, cl.(12), I.p.C, is wide enough and includes every person who is appointed to any office for the performance of some public duty. [688 B C] (v) The expression "Public servant" includes a public official. Therefore, an officer of the Corporation within the terms of section 6(1)(c) of Act, can be said to be public servant under section 21(9), cl. 12 of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958.

The appellant was convicted for contravention of r. 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order 1964. In appeal by special leave it was contended that r.141(2), which is within the powers conferred by section 3(1 ) of the Act, does not contain any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juar 's right to make a complaint under cl. (3) of that order and that r, 141(1) is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The High court was not justified in holding that r., 141(a) is within its powers. Rule 141(ii) is outside the powers under section 3 (1 ) and therefore, the order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture is ultra vivos. [272 G] In the instant case, the High court had set aside the conviction for contravention under cl 3 of that Order and instead of the sentences awarded by the lower courts sentenced the accused to imprisonment already undergone. The High 'Court was therefore justified in modifying the sentence passed on the appellant and instead directing the forfeiture of the juars seized from the house of the appellant. [273 G] The order of forfeiture is not ultra vires as it lays a rule contrary to the law contained under section 114, Evidence Act, and therefore the order cannot be set aside.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Sia was not in any manner concerned with the deep seated enmity between the appellant and the deceased, and that he had been falsely implicated by the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court, in favour of Siya Ram and his companions. [475E] (2) The circumstances show that the appellant was a colleague of the deceased and his associates. There is nothing on record to show that he was aware of the nefarious design of S iichani. It is not enough if he had known that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [775G] (3) The fact that the deceased was a fleeting holes, that he did not know the neces sary design of the Sia. It was also not enough that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happened to facilitate the commission of the crime. [771B C] (4) The circumstance that the High Court had relied on the evidence of Om Prakash Dubey in order to hold that Shri Ram had played an important role in the murderous design, is sufficient to sustain the conviction of Sya Ram.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that it was doubtful whether any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 304 Part I, Part II, Penal Code. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were not identified but only named persons, they did not take part in the murder. The evidence was adduced to prove that the said persons along with others named or unnamed, participated jointly in the crime. The fact that the other three accused were acquitted by the trial court did not lead to any conclusion that the appellant had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unidentified persons for committing the said offence. (ii)The High Court found that although accused 1 3 and four others were acquitted, they were convicted under s. 302 readwith section 34, of the Penal Code, though the other two accused were convicted only under section 307 read with s.34, of that Code. The appellant was therefore guilty under section 324 read with Section 34 of that code. (iii)The conviction and sentence passed by the High Court were not justified on the evidence adduced in this case. (iv)The appellant had been acquitted under section 27 of the Evidence Act. The judgment of the High court could not stand. (v)The appeal must be allowed. (vi)The judgment of acquittal was based on circumstantial evidence and it was not necessary to prove the same.

The petitioner, a citizen of India, filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental rights. The respondents, however, did not take any action against the petitioner. The petitioner filed an appeal before the Customs and Excise Authorities under Section 128 of the . The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal on the ground that there was breach of fundamental right. The High Court held that the petitioner had no fundamental right to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that (i) the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse; and (ii) the respondents had not taken any action under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The customs authorities are right in holding that no question of the enforcement of a fundamental right arises in article 32 of India. [626C] 1.2 In view of the aforesaid, it is clear that relief under Article 226 of the Constitu tion is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [625D] 1:3. The remedy under Article32 is wholly inapplicable to the facts of this instant case. It has further to be reiterated that for enforcement Of fundamental right which is dependent upon adjudication or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it will not automatically involve breach of the fundamental right for the enforcement thereof. [650E F] 1 :4. The relief under article 32 is wholly unnecessary in view of section 15(1)(b) of the , which provides that the rates of duty and tariff valuation if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the dates on which goods are actually removed or removed from such warehouse. [656F G] 1 5. The provisions of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot be said that there is breach of a right.
