Whenever a person complains and claims that there has been a violation of law, it does not automatically involved breach of any fundamental right, for the enforce ment of such rights depends on interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a statute for whom elaborate procedure was pre scribed. [646G H] 1 6. The Court is clearly of the opinion that relief contemplated by Article 32 is entirely inappropriate in this case and the application does not lie under Article 12 of the Consti tution.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of a bungalow. The sale was confirmed by the Court of Wards and the sale was set aside on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability of the sons to discharge the debts of their father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on pious obligation of the son who has been receiving a monthly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in execution of the payment order. [44 C] (ii) The debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the share of the appellants did not pass to the auction purchasers. [45 D] (iii) The High Court erred in holding that what could legally be sold under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code was the right, title and interest of the defaulter i.e. of the father alone which could not include the share in the other members of the joint family. [46 E F] (iv) The obligation of a son to discharge debts of his father does not cease merely because he has received a monthly salary or remuneration from a bank and the property is sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end. [47 F G] (v) The legal position is that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and (1) A.I.R. (2) (1878) L.R 14 I.A. i. (3) A,I. R. (4) All. 953, followed. (vi) The right, ownership or interest of a judgment debtor is based upon the pious duty of the children to discharge their debts and that the property was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of the decree holder which were characterised as "unamiable property" within the meaning of section 155(1) of the Act.

The petitioners, who were the police officers of Delhi Administration and the police officials, were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420, 468, 471 read with section 34 I.P.C., for having committed various offences punishable under sections 109/109/109 I. P.C. The prosecution alleged that the petitioners along with others had entered into a conspiracy to cheat the Government of India and to cheat them in respect of certain properties. The petitioners were charged under section 120B read with Section 34 I P. C. for having caused wrongful gain to themselves by using forged documents, forged documents etc., and also for causing wrongful loss to the Government. The Committee found that the accused had committed offences punishable u/s 109/10/109 of I.p.C.; that they were not guilty of any offence under section 8 B of the Act; that they had failed to account for the loss caused to the government by using the forged documents and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 178 I.PC. The committee, therefore, recommended the transfer of the petitioners in these cases to the Delhi Administration. The Delhi Administration filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the aforesaid order of the Committee. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Committee had not properly considered the case of the accused and that the prosecution was barred by section 8B of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section8 B of I P C; (ii) the proceedings before the Committee were vitiated because they had not been given an opportunity to defend themselves and (iii) the action of the committee in asking them to be cross examined at the end of the inquiry was discriminatory. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Committee should not have in the circumstances of the case directed the filing of a complaint against either of the Petitioners for an offence under sections 178 I P and 8 C. [522B] 1.2 The Committee shall have considered the conduct of various police officers, and in particular among others among others, among others whether the witnesses were similarly placed at the conclusion of the enquiry or not. If three persons referred to above to whom notices under section 13 B have been issued are to be examined even according to the Committee at the close of the proceedings, there is no justifiable reason to deny them treatment to the petitioners. [525C D] 1:3 The Committee would have then asked them to give evidence along with other material before it. If the Committee has found that they are covered under section8B then certainly they would not have been asked to get into witness box for being cross examined till the end. The affidavits and other material which were before the committee show that there were a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the Commis sioner.

The petitioners, who were seven in number, challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8(i) of the Rules, by which they were exempted from payment of lump sum in lieu of tax on fares and freights. The petitioners contended that the Act was unconstitutional as it imposed unreasonable restrictions on their fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19 (1)(g) of Constitution and that the impugned Act infringed articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31(2) and 301 of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of R.8(i), which are in conflict with the provisions contained in section 3 of the Act, are unconstitutional as offending article 19(6) of our Constitution. The Act and the Rules framed thereunder are not ultra vires the State Legislature. The tax is still on passengers and goods, though what it is to be is deter mined by the amount of fare or freight. The levy is therefore without authority of law. The provisions of the R. and the notification are valid. The State of Rajasthan vs Sri Ram Narain, ; , followed. The Punjab Passengers and goods Taxation Act, 1959 and the Notification issued thereunder were challenged as unconstitutional on the ground that it was discriminatory and ultra vires. The contention that the tax is without authority, because, under the Act it is optional, and involves payment of tax even when no passengers or goods are transported, cannot be accepted. The proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax payable on fares or freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. The notification does not cease to be a tax on passengers but only terminates the journey from one point to another. The word "tax" is used in the context of the provisions relating to taxation and it cannot be said that the Legislature intended to make a distinction between the tax on goods and the tax which is imposed on passengers, though the amount is measured by the fares and the freights, and therefore, the tax was beyond the Act by making the lump sum payment compulsory. The expression "taxes" in section 2(1) of that Act includes taxes on passengers. The words "tax on passengers" are not defined in the Act but only those which are imposed as a tax or as a fee for the purpose of taxation. The definition of "taxation" in the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act is wide enough to include all taxes levied under the State Acts and the rules made thereunder. The fact that the word "fee" is not defined by the Act does not mean that it is not a tax. The Legislature has not used the expression "fee". The tax, however, is still a tax in respect of passengers and Goods. The distinction between a tax and a fee is not admissible because the tax may be optional but involves payment for services rendered. The difference between the two is not an essential element of taxation but is one of fact depending on the circumstances of each case. The question whether a tax is imposed under the Entry, and if so, what is the nature of the tax, does not arise. The power to levy taxes is derived from the provisions in the Constitution itself and it is the duty of the Court to see that the taxes are not imposed without authority. The Court cannot strike down the law merely because it has no application to a case where the tax has been imposed by the State legislature. The validity of a tax can be challenged only if it is discriminatory or ultra vires, but not otherwise. The Constitution does not contemplate any discrimination between persons similarly situated and those who are similarly situated.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The workmen were retrenched from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour Court directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The appellant challenged the award in this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective on the date when they were sought to be retrenched. [567F] (2) The Labour Court has awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to he raised. [568F G] (3) The award shall stand modified accordingly. [569G H] (4) The direction for reinstatement is not a regular court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. [570A B] (5) The only limited question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back Wages to the respondents workmen. [571C D] (6) The High Court has not exercised its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 but has exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with the Award. [573F G; 571A B, E] (7) The question whether the workmen should be awarded full or partial back wages is no more open to challenge. It is no longer open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. [574F G, 571A] (8) The Award shall stand accordingly modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the sacrifice on management 's part too.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the conviction and death sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that the deceased was last seen in the company of the accused in the house of the deceased; (ii) the evidence of the doctor who conducted the postmortem examination of the dead body could not be put in evidence under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the same was inadmissible in evidence. HELD : (i)(a) The prosecution had proved beyond any doubt that it was the accused and none else who was responsible for the murder. [11 D] (b) The fact that the accused alone was with him at the time when he visited the house was not a circumstance which could be taken into consideration in judging his guilt. [12 E] (c) The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that there was no other person responsible for murder and the High Court had rightly confirmed the death sentence imposed by the trial court. [13 G] (d) The accused had not been convicted under section 201 Indian Penal Cods for committing murder of the wife of the first appellant. There is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder or that the relations of the son with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. [14 F] (e) The High court has rightly confirmed that the death of the daughter was caused by a sudden provocation and not by an unchaste wife.

The plaintiff sued for recovery of a sum of Rs. 80,507 7 8 being the aggregate amount due and payable by him under the mortgage deed dated 12th June 1936. The defendants pleaded that each of them was liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal reversed the decree holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove a contract to the contrary, and that the defendants were entitled to recover only Rs. 20,000 as the aggregate sum due and not Rs. 40,253 11 10 8 being interest due on that amount at the contract rate in the mortgage from the date of payment to the date on which the decree was passed. The plaintiff appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The suit was barred by section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the Contract Act, and the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for sale of the mortgaged property. The suit had been rightly decreed by the High court. (ii)The suit was not barred by limitation as it was filed within one year from the accrual of the cause of action. The period of limitation prescribed by section 82 is three years. The time taken in obtaining the decree must be excluded in computing the period of two years. (iii)The plaintiff had not used the word "subrogation" he has asked in substance for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs, 20,006 7 8 with interest against either defendant, I would direct that his liability be reduced to Rs. 2,500 and that his liabilities be reduced accordingly. (iv)The words "subjectively" in section 82 are wide enough to include the words "for the aggregate sums due" and not "for any sum which may be legally recoverable from either defendant. The words "in respect of the whole of the property" in the section mean that the decree in a mortgage suit shall (1) A.I.R. 1949 P.C. 65, (2) A,I. R. 1949 Mad. 829, (3) A.,I.L.R, 1949 Mad, 829 and (4) A ,of the same kind as section 82. The word "Subrogation " is used in a wider sense to include all kinds of transactions which are not covered by the provisions of section 92. In the present case the plaintiff 's suit was clearly barred by time.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The appointments were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment by Selection) Rules, 1973. The appellants applied for the posts of Assistant Engineers, and they were selected in the open competition. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Suppl. S.C., 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, [1988) Suppl. SCC, 657, relied on. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violationof the decisions laid down by this Court. [497C] 1.2 The Rules were clearly in contravention of the ratio laid down in Ashok Yadav & Anr. vs state of Haryana and Ors., ; , and Mohinder Singh Garg vs Union of India & Ors,, J.T. on 4th September, 1991. [498F G] 1:3. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [500G H] 1 :4. The Rules have been clearly in breach of the dictum laid down for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clear in violation thereof.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the prosecution has failed to prove conspiracy; (ii) the evidence of conspiracy is exculpatory in nature and, therefore, would not be admissible against the co accused; (iii) the High Court erred in holding that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [415C] 2.1 In the instant case, the prosecution witnesses have not spoken about any confession. They have also stated that they were meeting Sadanand at the jail. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadhanand on the night of occurrence following the incident, the Collector was not found there. It is well settled that the confession of co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In the present case, Sadanand had continuously been detained for meeting Sadarayan and his brother, P.W.4 on 11th April, 1983. The defence has also led evidence that after arrival of the deceased, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they had been meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [413D E] 2:2 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ques tion in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. The conclusion drawn by the High court, therefore cannot be sustained. [414F G] 3.1 The prosecution case has been corroborated by the evidence led by the prosecution and the defence witnesses. It has further come out that during the course of investigation, the story of bribing the jail officials was introduced. The State should also have taken some more care to see that everywhere in the police station is plugged. This kind of evidence cannot be accepted. [416H; 415A] 3:2. In a criminal case involving murder of a District Magistrate, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a person who was not present when the crime was committed following the raid on the Ashram. The trial court has failed in not properly appreciate the evidence and has not given any reasons for holding that it had no jurisdiction to take a view different from what has been stated about him by the trial court. [ 415C D] 3 :3. In such circumstances, the conviction of the appellant is not sustainable. [ 416D E; 417A] 4:1. The evidence of the prosecution witness on this score should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand was taken into custody following the search of the Ashram, better investigation had been expected and he had taken great pains to ensure the same. This is a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accept.

The appellant company was a textile mill and its workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. The company had to pay dearness allowance in accordance with the formula laid down by the Industrial Tribunal for fixing wage scales. In doing so the Tribunal took into account the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowance for subordinate staff. The Tribunal also observed that it would be open to the Tribunal to fix the same rates of dearness allowances for factory workmen as for clerical staff. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was right in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance. The principle therefore applied to the case of clerical staff and factory workmen. [365 E F] (ii) The financial capacity of the company to pay the minimum wage packet including basic wages fixed by it as well as dearness allowance fixed by the Tribunal was not disputed. The financial position of the appellant company is that its employees are not engaged in the same line of industry; they are not employed in any particular area carrying on the same business; and the Tribunal has not considered what would be the total wage packet for the purpose of fixing wages, and dearness allowances. [366 E F]. (iii) The principle of fixing wage scale is based on the principles laid down in the Industrial Disputes Act and the principles applicable to industrial adjudication. The principles which are relevant for fixing the wage scales are: (a) that there should be a uniform pattern of dearness pay for clerical and subordinate staff; (b) that the minimum wages fixed under the Act should be higher than the minimum; (c) that it should have done so in respect of all categories of employees; (d) that in fixing such scales of pay, the Tribunal must not only take into account all relevant factors but also take into consideration all other relevant circumstances including the trend in that region. [367 E G] (iv) The principles laid out by the Supreme Court in the case are applicable to the present case. The appellant company had been paying the highest wages in respect Of all categories in comparable concerns and it was not possible to fix any higher wage packet with respect to clerical staff as compared to the employees of the other comparable concerns. [368 E] (v) The formula laid out for fixing pay scales is a rational one and has to be applied with reference to the relevant factors. The method adopted by the tribunal in fixing wages is not arbitrary or capricious. [369 G H] (vi) The basis on which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter was that there were different scales of dearness Allowance for clerical employees and factory employees. It had also been urged that the pattern of wage packet should be uniform throughout the country and that it was necessary to keep in view the trends in the region and fix the minimum rates of wages for factory workers as for industrial workmen. The tribunal had not considered whether the total number of workmen in comparable concern would be sufficient to make the comparison. [370 G H; 371 A] (vii) The Industrial Tribunal has put the subordinate staff in the similar position as those of the clerical and sub staff. It has also been pointed out that the Tribunal should have followed this pattern.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Bombay. The respondents filed a suit against the appellants for redemption of the mortgage and possession of the lands on the ground that they were agriculturists, that the appellants had no right to redeem them as the mortgagors had not been made parties to the suit; that the suit was barred by limitation under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal held that the Rajinama was a complete relinquishment of his interest and that the respondents were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. On appeal by special leave, Held, that section 74 was not applicable to the present case as the appellants were agriculturists and the respondents could not claim redemption of Shiddappa 's one half share in the suit land. The Rajinma was the registered occupant and the Rajinspec tively did not purport to transfer the interest of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that is, the appellants ' right to get possession by adverse possession was extinguished and that as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse Possession. Held, further, that under section 73 of the Act the Rajenama was only a complete relinquish ment of his rights and did not create any relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers. The appellants had not merely an interest in the land but also a right to have it partitioned. The suit was therefore barred by time.

The respondent, a manufacturer of stencil paper, was assessed to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 on the ground that carbon paper was not "paper" as defined in the Act and was liable to sales Tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to the end of March 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal which held that the carbon paper did not lost its character because it was not a paper as defined by the Act. On further appeal, the High Court held that it was a paper which was used for printing, writing or printing, or for packing, or in any other manner, and that the respondent was entitled to claim that carbon Paper should be taxed at the rates specified in Schedule I to the notification and that it could not be said that ribbons were "paper other than hand made paper". The High Court also held that there was no force in the contention of the appellant that carbon copy was not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter. In appeal by certificate, the appellant contended: (1) that carbon copies were not " Paper other than Hand made paper" as used in Notification No. Sales tax Act, 1947; (2) that ribban was not paper within the meaning of Entry 2 of the Notification and therefore the turnover could not he subjected to salestax at the time and at 6%. HELD: (i) The mere fact that the word "paper " forms part of an denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838C] (ii) The word " paper" in the common parlance or in the com plaints, is not determinative of the questions whether the articles are paper as ordinarily understood. The mere possibility that the words used in the Notification are not identical with those used in notification No. sales tax Act 1948, does not make it clear that the expression "paper ' has not been defined either in the U .P. General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1966 or in U. P. Sales Act, 1957. [889D E] (iii) The use of the word 'paper ' in Notification Nos. 1 and 2 of 1966 is not conclusive of the matter whether the goods are paper other than " hand made Paper". It is only aviation petrol that is used for bearing, writing, or printing or for making packing or for drawing on, or by cover ing the walls. [899E F] (iv) The High Courts have held that in popular parlance, the word has been used as meaning a sub stance which is used to bear the name of a particular type of art or art. It is not necessary that the name should be given in the definition of "paper". [888F G] (v) The expression " paper other then" in Notification 8/66 dated July 1. 1966, does mean paper which is capable of bearing writing or packing.

The appellant was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. It had its head office at Hapur and it had its branches at Hapur. The respondents were employed by the owners of the appellant Mills at Hapur in the year 1955. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents from service on the ground that they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thereby they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. 1 of the company. The appellant challenged the legality of this order by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Allahabad. The High Court held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1 to 4 had disobeying their orders of transfer, they were properly dismissed. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the right to transfer an employee by an employer from one concern to another is implicit in every contract of service; (2) that there is no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant has the right of transfer to another place, and (3) that even if the appellant had such an intention, the respondents had knowledge of the same. HELD : The appeal must be dismissed. The employer in the present case has no such right. It is not a condition of service of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the employer has the inherent right to transferred his employee to another. [922 B] The question whether an employee had the right under Standing order No. I of the Company to transfer him to another, was essentially one of fact to be decided on the facts of each case. It was not a question of law which arose in the case and that raised by the appellant was not one of law. [936 C] The employer has no power to transfer his employee if he has the rights under Standing Orders 1, 2 or 3 of the Act. The Standing Order does not provide for any such right but only lays down that the employee should serve in a particular concern. It does not prohibit the employer from transferring an employee if the right is conferred on him by Standing Order 1.2 or 3.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948 as a limited company. The respondent, the principal employer of the appellant company, was incorporated on July 1, 1948 under the . It had its registered office at Bombay and its branches at Ahmedabad. The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V were in force. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended and it includes among other items, (i) payment of contributions and provision of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and (ii) payment by the employer 's State Insurance Fund. The appellant company claimed that the contribution payable under Chapter V A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant. The claim was rejected by the respondent, who held that the contributions were not liable to be taxed in respect of factories or establishment situated in the areas in question. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant against the order of the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the payment of contribution directed to be made by the employers under the or other similar payment or benefit under various other social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service and conferment of an advantage to the employer or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. [1088C] 2. The expression "any other matter" in section 28 lists II and III contain several entries in respect thereof. It is not disputed that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. For a start the scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the case of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the cases of employers, who do not yet receive the benefit of the scheme, its rate of contributions is lower. This contribution goes to a fund known as the Employees ' State Inspec tive Fund which is to be utilised for the benefits to be given to the employees under the Act. [1189F G] 3. The object of the Act is to provide a fee for the acquisition of an insurance scheme and it is not possible for the legislature of any State, subject to conditions with which we are not concerned, to decide in what areas and in respect to which factories or factories should be established. It does not require that the employer must have the benefit or advantage of the provisions contained in the Act, but will be entitled to make a contribution under section 28 of the . [1190G H] 4. The scheme is limited to a certain area and though Special contribution is leviable from all employer wherever they are, in tho case of factories who straightaway receives the benefits under the scheme. their rate is higher than that in the other cases. [1291A B] 5. The question whether special contribution should be indirect or remote has to be decided on the facts of each case and not by applying the general principles of 'the Act. The fact that special contribution was levied from the employees who straightaway received the benefits would not make any difference because the employers ' contribution under the , constitutes only a fee, and not a tax. [1391B C] 6. The Government cannot go on levying employers ' contributions under section 2(g) of the , as it does not provide for rendering any services or conferment of such benefit to employees as may be quid pro qua for the payments. [1491C D] 7.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services as daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands were of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management, however, did not give them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. The petitioners filed writ petition challenging the order of their absorption and the High Court rejected their claim and came to the following conclusion: "The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, they are surplus to the establishment as on 31st March, 1988. They are being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work available for them". The petitioners challenged the aforesaid order before this Court by way of a writ petition. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regularly workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [610G H] 2. The principles of regularisation are applicable to the case of the petitioners. They have been working on rolls and paid in spite thereof. On these facts, the question of directing their absorption or regu larisation does not arise. [625H; 621A B] 3. The doctrine of regularisation is applicable only when there is no work for them. In fact, the petitioners are being given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. [650B C] 4. The concept of regularisation has been evolved by this Court in several decisions. It has been stated that the principle of regularised of a regularly workman is applicable to cases where the daily wages are paid on the basis of an ad hoc appointment or on the recommendations of an Industrial Tribunal or Labour Court or when an industrial dispute is pending before it. [643C D] 5. The practice of regularisation in such cases has been deprecated by this court. [641D] 6. The scheme of voluntary retirement has been framed which is Annexure R V to the counter affidavit. This document shows the amount of retrenchment compensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated workers under this Scheme. The said document shows that the petitioners being surplus to their establishment as a result of the closure of the industry, they have been continued on rolls. [651D E] 7. The plea of regularisation cannot be accepted. The Court has not found any ground to interfere with the High court 's decision in view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the Petitioners and that for quite some time they have not agitated their claim.

The appellants were the plaintiffs in a suit for possession of certain properties. The respondents contended that the sale was not real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh, but only to the extent of 2 1/2 as share belonging to them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants had failed to prove their right to the property and that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0. r. 8(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure from questioning the validity of the mortgage of the entire interest effected by them under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellants could not be allowed to raise the plea of estoppel against the respondents and set aside the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) when by the sale in execution of a mortgage decree obtained by the National Agency Co., the co heirs were estopped from questioning its validity, the plaintiffs could not raise any specific plea touching their right or title to the properties; and (2) even assuming that the transaction was real and effective to pass the title to them, it would stand on the same footing as the sale of the property in execution passed by a court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained in a civil suit.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the conviction and sentence on the ground that the omission to comply with the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with by the police officer in charge of the investigation. Held, that the failure to comply the provisions Of section 173(1) of Code of criminal Procedure was fatal to the trial. The omission to do so did not affect the validity of the trial unless it was shown that the accused had been prejudiced in his defence. The defect in the trial was curable by reference to section 537 of the code, as no case of prejudice had been made out against the accused. The provisions of section 537(3), Cr. P.C., were mandatory and not directory. The failure to do that would render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. The fact that the appellant got the necessary copies of the depositions of the witnesses in the Sessions Court before the statements of the prosecution witnesses were recorded by that court, did not make any difference as regards the non compliance with the requirements of section 173 (1) Cr. As the omission was curing to comply within the time allowed by the trial court, it could not be said that the irregularity was cable. The irregularity was cured by reference only to section 540(3). The fact of prejudice having been caused to the accused by the non supply of copies of depositions of witnesses in his Sessions Court did not render the proceeding including the examination of the defence witnesses vitiated. The trial had not proceeded on the basis that the omissions were curable and the irregularity could be cured by resort to section 233(4). The omission was not a defect which was celled out by reference under section 537 Cr. The appellant was therefore entitled to have his case heard in accordance with law.

The appellant Municipality, which was constituted under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, had been directed to stop the discharge of effluents in the manner specified in the notice issued by it. The respondent Municipality filed a petition for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the appellant not to take any action against the respondent Municipality for failure to comply with the requisition made by it under section 153A(1) of the Act. The High Court held that the provisions of section 153 A were ultra vires and void as it would be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right conferred on the citizens by article 19(1)(C) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of sections 153A and 153A are not intended for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. They are designed to achieve the purpose of preventing a nuisance which may be caused by the discharge or otherwise of the effluent. [395 D] (ii) The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective opinion of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge and the discharge. The purpose of the section is to enable the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists, to issue a notice requiring the person to whom the notice is given to show causes why he shall not be ordered to arrange the discharge thereof in the way specified in sub section. [397 D E] (iii) The purpose for which the notice has been issued is to give an opportunity to the person concerned to show that the nuisance in question exists and to agree to comply therewith, and if the existence or absence of a complaint is assumed because that was a matter for the determination of the Municipal Court, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire into the dispute. [398 E F] (iv) The provision of section 154(1), which provides that no person shall be liable to any penalty under this Act for failure or neglect to comply within the prescribed period, is inconsistent with the provisions contained in section 153B and is not repugnant to article 19 of the Constitution.

The appellant was found in possession of certain goods. The police recovered from him a large number of parts of railway machinery and kept them in 11 bags. The appellant 's explanation that the goods were being used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway was not accepted by the trial court as correct. The High Court dismissed his bail bond but on appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution must prove that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise. HELD: (i) The prosecution must also establish that the article seized were Railway stores within its meaning. [192 G] (ii) The appellant was not called upon to prove that goods were railway property within the definition of section. [195 B C] (iii) The evidence in this case did not establish that articles seized from the appellant were railway properties within the purview of section 3. [196 F] (iv) The seizure of the goods was effected by the police and not by the appellant himself. [197 G] In the present case, the search which took place in the presence of the appellant and the manager of the transport company revealed that a large quantity of parts were contained in 23 bags of metal scrap booked the same day by the appel lant for consignment to Jullunder. The evidence did not prove that articles were railway assets within the description of section ' 2 of Act. [198 G] Moyalal Rostagir vs The State, ; , followed. (v) The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to establish that they were the property of a Railway Administration.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondent on the ground that they had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate court affirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the judgments of the courts below and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants are entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or compromise is established. [10E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not been able to prove that the appellants were tenants within the meaning of section 2(1)(iii) of the Act. The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised property governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to their rights in the tenancy rights in respect of commercial premises. [11F G] 1:3. The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of tenants in respect thereof, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs should be deemed to have been substituted for the heirs in the contractual lease. [12G H] 1 :4. In the present case, it was held that the tenant who continues to remain as a statutory tenant after the termination of his contractual tenancy till a decree for ejectment against him is passed, continued to have an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises and tenancy rights therein are heritable. Therefore, the appellants succeeded before the courts to the extent of their right to remain In possession even though they succeeded to tho heritable interest. [13H; 14A] 1 5. The High Court was not justified in interfering with the judgments and decrees of the Courts below.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Employees Provident Fund Scheme, 1952 to all its workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees ' Provident Fund Act applies. The employees also submitted their claims for bonus and gratuity. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees provident fund Act. The Tribunal held that the benefit of the Provident Fund was not extended to any additional categories of workmen, but only to those who were covered by the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Government is the financier of the Boards and the employees contribute equally. It was further contended that the Board has no power to extend or reduce the benefits under the Provident fund Act to any other class of workmen. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion while it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the employer. [47 D] The Board has to carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [48 E] The Provident Fund Commissioner is directed to take into account the financial capacity of the industry as well as the fact that the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employers.

The respondent husband filed a petition for maintenance under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate passed an order of maintenance to the wife and directed her to pay Rs. 500/ per month as maintenance from the date of application till the date she was actually paid. The respondent filed revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the woman to refuse her to live in the husband 's house and hence she is not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live at the husband merely because her husband was impotently placed under the influence of her husband, and that this salutary provision which was introduced with the clear object of arming the wife with a cause of action for refusing to live separately from her husband ', should be regarded as just ground or reasons for the husband to refuse the wife 's refusal to live together with her father.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for declaration of his title and for possession of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. The defendant contended that by virtue of these orders the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had been transferred to the State of Saurashtra, the Government of Saurashtra recognised the said Resolutions dated 19th January 1948 and 29th February 1948 as being binding on the plaintiff. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of any portion of the property. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that the title to the suit land was never recognised by the Union of India or the State Government and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show that as early as July 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of the erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Ministry of the Union. The High Court also held since the plaintiff had not shown possession of these lands within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit for possession based on title to that property and the defendants had denied title. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the State had admitted the ownership of the lands in question and the structures vested in the Defence Department from the date of Financial merger and when the State took over the land, there was nothing on record to show as to how the Municipality was formally handed over the lands. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff has not shown that the Municipality is formally handedover the land in question, that its right over the suit premises and the buildings known as Rasala Lines are not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the written statement they did not claim the structures as belonging to the Municipality. [232G] 2. The State Government has corrected themselves in their communication dated 6th May, 1952 and stated that the claim of the plaintiff that the lands were vested in it was erroneous and that it had no jurisdiction to give a finding on title of the appellant even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. [231A] 3. The fact that the Government had corrected themselves did not mean that the land was vested in its full sense, but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the land. In the instant case, the Resolution No. 77 dated 29th Feb., 1948 by which the entire property was transferred to them by the orders of their Highness, Bhavnagar, State in 1948 and they are collecting the Revenue from the farmers. As seen earlier, possession of lands was also not taken by the Municipali ty at any time. In fact, it may be mentioned that the government of Saurashtra had corrected itself in their communications dated 6 5 1952 and 7th May 1952 and that they were collecting the revenue from the agriculturists. [234B C] 4.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Indian Penal Code. He was charged with having committed an offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947, and was convicted by the Judicial Commissioner. The Judicial Commissioner on appeal affirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of fine. On a reference made by the High Court of Bombay, the Judicial Commis sioner held that the appellant was not an officer within the definition of section 2(9), Indian Penal code and therefore he was not a public Servant within the mischief of section 3 Of Act II Of 1947. The appellant contended that the words "any person" in section 21 (9) were wide enough to include all railway servants from the definition, and that the provisions of section 137 of the Railways Act did not exclude all railway employees from the purview of the Act. Held, that an officer in the service or pay of Government performing as such a public duty entrusted to him by the Government and was therefore a public servants within the scope of section 6(1) Of the Indian Railway Act IIof 1947. Section 21 (10) of Indian Railways Act, 1890, which declared "every officer in any service or payment of Government" to be a public officer, was not ultra vires the Constitution. The words "other than a railway servant" in s.21(9)(a) were comprehensive enough to cover all railway officers and servants within its scope. The word "officer" used in section 6 (1) of Madras Act II, 1947, meant "any other person performing public duty". The appellant was therefore an officer of the Government within the terms of section 1(9).

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for recovery of a sum of Rs. 17,794/6/6 as arrears of land revenue due from him on account of the sale of his share in the property. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court and the first appellate court upheld the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the portion of the building standing on the said plot of land was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court also held that a part of the said building was exempted from attachment, and sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Appellants that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from the attachment and sales under clause(ccc), but was in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery, of revenue due to the State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment levied on and the auction sale notified in respect of the Respondent 's half share in a property was not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance thereof. [848C] 2. Section 60(1) provides that where an attachment or sale is made under the provisions of the Act, the following particulars shall not be liable to such attachment or sales, namely: (a) name and address of the judgment debtor; (b) the amount due from the judgment debtors on account thereof; (c) the date on which the sale was held; (d) the name and addresses of the parties to the suit; (e) the names and addresses as the sites and the land immediately appurtenant thereto and necessary for their enjoyment; (f) the time at which the attachment or the sale is held; and (g) any other particulars which may be prescribed. [884C D] 3. The words "such attachment or Sale" in the proviso are wide enough to include the attachment of property under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. The opening words of sub section(1), however, refer to the attachment,and sale mentioned in sub section.(1) thereof. The expression "such attached or sale" in clause (c), is not restricted to execution and sale of any of its statutes made expressly apply thereto. [881D E] 4. Section 61 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1939 provides that the provisions contained in sections 60 and 60 shall not apply to an attachment and sell under any other law for the time being in force. The proviso to section 60(I) is clear and unambiguous and does not require that the words "or any other provision" in sub s.(1), must be read as including a provision which would not be applicable to an attached or sold property. [89F G] 5. Section 59 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that no sale shall be deemed to take place without the previous permission of the Court and unless such permission is given, the property is liable to attachment and sold in execution thereof. It does not say that the expression "or other provision of law made expressly or by necessary implication applicable thereto" would include a provision for exemption from attachment. [90G H] 6.

The respondent, a retired Government servant, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1957 58 and 1958 59. The appellant 's claim for compensation under section 23(1)(a) of the , was rejected by the Special Deputy Collector on the ground that the value of the lands in question had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as at the date of death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. The respondent 's appeal against the order of assessment was dismissed by the Assistant Collector, who held that the valuation of the land in question was not correct and that the appellant had no right to claim compensation for the lands acquired by the Government. The High Court upheld the view of the Assistant Collec tor. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands still formed part of the estate of the deceased and that having regard to the glaring enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the land, the said lands had escaped assessment to excise duty; (ii) the High Court was wrong in holding that the respondent 'rejected the claim on the wrong assumption that it had been passed on the basis of the valuation made by the special Deputy Collector. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in its conclusion that the notice issued under section 59(a) would have been valid if the same had been issued on the strength of compensation awarded by the civil Court and not on the foundation on which the same was issued. [334C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent did not estimate the market value of lands acquired and as such it was not a case of change of opinion on his part as regards the correct valuation of lands. The claim for compensa tion under section 73A was rejected on the erroneous assumption that the acquired lands still form part of estate of deceased and the same having been undervalued in view of glaring enhanced compensa tions, the High court had attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant cases the respon dents had merely accepted the value as determined by the other authority namely the City Civil Court. [330D E] 1:3. The question whether a particular land is liable to be assessed to excise duties or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It cannot be disputed that when the original assessment was made it was the duty of the respondent, after scrutinising the account filed and examining the materials produced before him, to value the estate. [328H] 1 :4. The fact that the land had been assessed on the date when the Collector accepted the compensation fixed by the Collector did not represent their correct market value which was clear from the glaring increase in the compensation awarded to the respondent.

The appellant was elected as a Director of the Bank from the Brewery, Chandrapur District Central Cooperative Bank. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the bank from the said Brewery. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank Act, 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of that bank as per the provisions of section 73FF of the Act and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The Deputy Registrar, however, did not pass any order under section 77(1). The appellant challenged the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having ceased to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan before the notice was issued would not be material for taking action under section 79(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Act, 1961. [680B] 1.2 The disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21.10.86 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. [681C D] 1:3. The disqualification under section 73F(1), as a result of default, is common both for election and for continuation as a director in the Committee. The special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, and the disqualification as a consequence of his having committed default is extinguished and consequently the appellant is not at any stage eligible to challenge the election as a defaulter. [682F G] 1 :4. The word 'debt ' in section 73(1 ) of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act, 1925 has been used with reference to the person who has incurred the disqualification.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on September 1, 1977. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the order reducing the pension by 50% of his pension before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Govt 's order dated December 4. 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government has power to reduce the amount or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [33B] 1.2 In the instant case, the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. There was no dispute that the respondent had retired from the service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 30, 1977 and charges were served on him on October 16, 1978 after about a year of his retirement. [34C D] 1:3. The Government 's power to reducing the quantum of pension is not in doubt. It has power under Rule 189 to reduce or withhold the pension granted to a Government Servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service. This rule further provides that before any order reducing or withdrawing pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note 1 to Rule 33 of the said Rules. In the present case, there was no doubt that the Government had power to enhance the amount. [35E F] 2.1 A government servant who retired from a service on or after the completion of his service cannot escape the liability for misconduct and negligence or financial irregularities which he might have committed during the period of his serv ice and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension. [36F G] 2:2 The purpose of enquiry was to inflict punishment on a government servant depending upon the good conduct of the Government servant. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold, or withdraw any part of the pension payable under Rule 191 for misconduct, which he could have committed whilst in service or after completion of the period. [37F G; 38A] 2 :3. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not possible to hold that the order was malafide. The order was passed on December 3, 1982 and the State government had no power to take action against the Respondent.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's premises. The appellant filed an application under section 3(3) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for permission to sue his tenant. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the permission granted by him was invalid in law. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to eject the respondent from the premises. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the words "any person who is not a District Magistrate" in section 3 (4) read with section 16 are clear and unambiguous, and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil court is completely excluded in relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the Act; (ii) the word "any" used in section 2(g) of Act II of 1947, means "any persons who are not District Magistrate". The High court held that it was clear from the language of section 3 that the Commissioner had no power to pass an order on the application made by the landlord for permission. In this appeal by special leave, it was urged on behalf Of the appellants (i). that the words of section 2 (g) read together with section 3 and 16 are wide enough to include persons who were not District Magistrates; (2) that the word 'any ' in section 16(4) has been used in a wider sense than the word in section 15(1); (3) that section 3 had no application because the words 'any person ' have been used only in the same sense as in section 18 of the , and (4). HELD : (i)(a) The words "other persons" in sub section (2), read together, are clear enough to indicate that they are intended to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner. [563 D] (b) The word 'person ' has been defined in section 4(1) of U. P. Act II Of 1947 as including a person who was not a district Magistrate. Section 3(4), therefore, clearly indicates that the District Magistrate is empowered to grant permission to the landlord to sue the tenant. [564 E] (c) The language of sub section 2 of section 16 does not intend that before a District Magis trate grants permission to a landlord to file a suit against his tenant he shall issue notice to the tenant and give him an opportunity to represent his case before the application of the landlord is rejected. [565 G] (d) Section 3 (3), therefore. clearly indicates the intention of the legislature that the Collector has to hear the application under sub section 1 (3). The word "person" in this amended provision, means 'any persons ' and not 'any other person '. [567 A B] (ii)(a). The words 'other persons ' have to be read together and they are clear indication of that intention. [568 G H] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding that the notice issued by the Commissioner under section 2 was invalid.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as an Assistant Secretary to the Government of Punjab in January, 1973. He was promoted as Deputy Secretary to that Government on August 1, 1974. In July, 1975 he was promoted to the post of Joint Secretary to Government of India. On September 30, 1975, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of his promotion and also praying for a direction to the State Government to promote him from the date of his appointment as Joint Secretary. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence was inadmissible in evidence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before making the reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of the alleged misbehaviour of the respondent and that, therefore, the High court had no jurisdiction to make the reference. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this court under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service commission can only be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court has on inquiry reported to it that the President or such other member ought to be removed on any such ground. [642C D] 2. The question whether the report of the High Commissioner is an independent fact finding authority for the purpose of Article 317 (1) of the Constitution is not open to consideration by this Court in a reference made by the President under Article 318(1). [643E F] 3. It was contended that the case of his client is that he has been falsely implicated into the charge of assault because he had incurred the wrath of the Chief Minister of Punjab and the hostility of thejj 's husband and that it would be impossible for him to prove the case unless he is allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. [643F] 4. The evidence in this case was not recorded by the Judge, but by a court of first instance. It could not be said that the High Courts had no power to make reference to the Supreme court under article 317(2) of Constitution. [641A B] 5. The procedure which this Court should adopt in a Reference made by President under article 318 (1), is not in accordance with the requirement that he should first have been given an opportunity to cross examination on those matters. It is true that the Chief Justice may write to the Registrar of the Supreme or any member of his family but it is not necessary that he can be examined or cross examined as a witness, except with the leave of this Court. [651C D; 642E] 6. The word "person" in Article 317 has been used in contradistinction to "any person". It is not possible to define precisely what is meant by "person". In other words, it is an idle complaint that the witnesses who have filed affidavits in this Court may be summoned or requested by the learned Judge to attend his court for the purposes of cross examination. [ 643E] 7. The expression "any other person" in article 317 (2) has been interpreted in a wider sense and it has been held that it is only when an affidavit is tendered that the question whether a particular witness is guilty of misconduct or not would arise. [ 644F G] 8. It cannot be said, therefore that the word "Person" in section 2(1)(a) of Act means any person who has not filed an affidavit in this court.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. 1 of 1939), for a declaration that the trust deed dated June 30, 1948 executed by the deity installed in the temple was not a private one and the deity was installed in a temple by the members of the public or their descendants. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the endowment was of a public nature and the idol installed in it was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the temple being a family temple, the deity must be regarded as a private and not a public endowment and that the mere fact that members of a community were allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members or the public had a right to worship in the Temple. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence to show that the deity did not make any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members of public. [830C] 2.1 The mere fact of worship would not determine whether the user of the temple by members, of the community is as of right; that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the dedication was of such a nature. [ 832E F] 2:2 In order to decide whether an endowment is of a private or of a Public nature it must be established that the intention of the testator or the founder was merely to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members thereof. The mere factum of worship will not determine the nature of the endowment. [883G] 2 :3 In order that a public trust may be inferred from the conduct of the parties it is necessary concomitant of the installation of the deity, and therefore, the mere factum or factum of service of the worship by members or their families, would not necessarily mean that the idol was of an ordinary nature. The fact that the family was allowed to enter the temple with the members belonging to the public would not be sufficient to establish the endowment as a public one. [881G H] 2 2:4 In order for determining whether an institution is of such nature, it must necessarily be established by evidence that the worship of the members and their families was as of necessity or of necessity. [851A B] 3. The finding of the High court that the property was dedicated to the deity is not a conclusive proof of dedication. It has been held that when property is dedicated for religious purposes, it is a private, and not an endowment. In the instant case, the evidence shows that the founder of the trust did not give any indication as to how the temple became extinct. The existence of the family deity was not decisive of the nature or character of the endowments. [871B C] 4. The question whether the endowment is a public or private one has to be determined with reference to the facts and circumstances of each case. [877C D] 5.

The appellant Bank was a contractor of the military and other authorities. The contract provided that the contractor would pay to the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills, and if the amount due under the bill was not paid within the stipulated time, the bank would be entitled to recover it from the appellant. The appellant Bank then filed a suit in the court of the Subordinate Judge against the respondent for recovery of certain amounts due under a contract entered into by it with the military. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decree holding that there was no equitable assignment of the moneys due under bills and that the appellant was not entitled to attach it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement between the appellant bank and the respondent was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant 's debts under the contracts. The power of attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 was a specific engagement by the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund coming to the debtor or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order directing such person to pay such funds to the creditor. [607 D E] (ii) The power conferred on attorney coupledwith the endorsement thereon on the bills dated July, 19,1948 was a general engagement by an agent to pay off the debts due under contracts and was irrevocable. The endorsement on bill dated 7th July 1948 was merely an express engagement by Malayalam for payment of money and did not confer any right on the appellant to attach the amount. [708 E F] (iii) The High Court was in error in holding that the respondent had no equitable assignmen of the fund by way of security. [777 G] (iv) The endorsement in the bill of 1948 was only an express agreement between Malhotra and the borrower and not a mere formal agreement. The words "any other person" in section 2(g) of the Act are clear enough to take in all transactions relating to the receipt of money or any interest on the amount receivable under bills. [779 C] (v) The word "person" in the context means a person who is entitled to receive money and includes a person whose property is sold or delivered in execution of a decree. [781 E F; 778 A] (vi) The words 'any other persons ' in section 3(g), are clear and unambiguous. The expression "any person" has been used in the sense in which it is used in section 4(1)(a). In the context of the definition of "person", it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, namely, Malhotra and Bank was that of borrower and lender and that, for the purpose of carrying out the terms of the contract, the debt due to the bank was paid out from a specific funds coming to his debtor or in the names of the bank in payment of such bills. The right of attorney holder coupled with endorsement on bills dated 7 7 1948 was not a clear agreement between him and the loanee. [780 E F]. (vii) The expression 'any person ' in the section means any person who has interest in the fund. The word 'person ' is used to denote a person, who is not entitled as an agent of a debtor. In the present case, the appellant had an interest in his fund and was merely authorised to act as his agent.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co., Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. Under that scheme, the appellant was to be paid Rs. 27,948/ as salary and allowances to its employees in addition to their salary. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources.
