The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions of sections 23(2), 28 and 67 of the Act were not applicable to the case as the Town planning Officer had no jurisdiction to determine the amount of compensation in the appellant ' s case. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act specifies a principle of compensation, that the market value of the original plots should be determined on the basis of the market price of the land at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme and published it in the prescribed manner. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Town Planning officer under section 32(1 (iii) has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plot included in the final scheme (which is not the final plot for brevity 's sake). [876G] 2. The provisions of section 67 of Act are applicable only to cases where the owner of an original plot is not provided with a plot in the Final scheme or if the contribution to be levied from him under section 66 is less than the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions thereof. [877C] 3. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land has to be determined by the local authority under clause(viii) of section 64 (1) or if he makes a claim before the Town Plan Officer within the prescribed time, and the amount by which the total value of plots exceeds the value of original plots with all the buildings and works thereon of such person shall be deducted from or added to, as the case may be, the contributions leviable from such person under section 67. [887D] 4. The principles for determining compensation are the same as in the present case. Under clause (xiii) the Town plan Officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner on the valuation of the plot used, allotted or reserved for a public purpose or purpose of the local Authority which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to tho general public, which shall be included in costs of the Scheme. The rate of interest payable by the owner under section 71 of the Bombay Town Planning and Development Act, 1948 is not less than that prescribed by the Act. [807E F] 5. The scheme is a self contained scheme and it is intended to provide for the payment of compensation to the general public in respect thereof. It is not possible to lay down any principle of valuation which would be applicable to all cases where there is no specific provision in the Act or in the rules made thereunder. [877G] 6. The object of the Town development scheme is to provide a uniform rate of compensation for land acquired by private persons and for matters connected therewith. It does not require that the owner should estimate the market rate of the value on the date on which the declaration of intent to make the scheme was made. [878A B] 7. The Act specifies the principles of compensation. The method of determining the amount to which the owner is entitled to compensation from section 71 is the basis whether an acquirer of land is given a reconstituted plot or not. [879E F; 886B] 8. The procedure for determination of compensation is prescribed by section 69 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Under section 69, the owner has to determine his market value on that basis. Section 69 provides that the net amount of loss shall be payable to the local authorities in cash or in such other manner as may be agreed upon by the parties.

The appellant was the third son of one Seetharama. The respondent 's brother died in 1934 leaving two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal held that the will was not genuine and that the testator had no male issue but left it to the legatee to decide whether the property should be divided in equal shares or not. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the words "he shall give to the female children" in section 89 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, are wide enough to include a son who is the guardian of three children and not a daughter who has no male issues but left only two daughters. The will does not say that the legatees were entitled to choose between the son and his wife. It merely says that the legatee should give the right of selection to the nearest heir, and it is not necessary for the testator to express any words from which it can be inferred that the bequest was in altogether void for uncertainty. The intention of the testator was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatee making the selection in the order in which they were named in the will. The words " he shall give" in the Will to the two daughters are not similar to the words used in the case of the foster son, but they are different in the cases of daughters as compared to the word "he may have". The intention was clearly expressed by the testator and it was not necessary that the word should be given a restricted meaning.

The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for joint possession of the plots in dispute, being co bhumidars. The defendants contested the suit and pleaded that the plaintiff was not in separate occupation of the land or plots in question and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit. The District Judge held that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of the zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants, and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The High Court also found that there was no evidence on record to prove that the appellant was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the defendants assured the plaintiff that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the Act, because the clear evidence of PW, Karbalai Begum, is to the effect that she was not at all informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of a co bhumidar under the Uttar pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Rules, 1950, is not a sine qua non for his acquisition of a right to hold property. [867G] 2. It is well settled that in order to establish a claim of adverse possession, the plaintiff must prove that he was in exclusive possession of all the properties and that he had been dispossessed by the defendant or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. [886A B] 3.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The first respondent filed an affidavit stating that he was a Minister of the Union and that he had been appointed as Deputy Prime Minis ters in the State Assembly. He also stated that he did not have any constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Ministers. The petitioner also stated in his affidavit that he would be paid Rs. 1,000 per month as salary to the Chief Minister. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the oath register was by incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Minis ter, he takes the same oath as the other ministers are required to take. He maintains that yet in view of his fact that the Constitution describing him as the Prime Minister, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Ministers and this practice is in vogue eversince 1951. The oath register is by the incumbent signed on as Prime Mini and all others sign as representatives. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction. [312E F] 1.2. In the affidavit of Respondent No 1 certain precedents have been relied upon and the practice which has been followed eversti ng the Constitution came into force has been referred to. The practice which had been followed by Respondent No1, some of the precedents have not been specifically stated in the affidavit. [313C D] Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , relied on.

The appellant was a public utility industry. The management of the appellant 's factory carried on a strike which took place in the course of the working day and it was alleged that the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to any holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, 1948. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the continuity of service of the workers was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers were not enti tled to annual holidays with wages under section 50 B (2) of that Act. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of holidays under section 48 B (I) of Factories Act. The Tribunal found on the evidence that there was no break in the continuity between the appellant and its workers and as a result the workers had lost their benefit of holiday on 1st November 1948. It also held that though the strike was illegal, it was not a lock out for a period of 12 months. Held, further, that in view of the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the discontinuance of work on 1th November, 1948 amounted to a break in continuity of the service of a workman concerned. The appellant was therefore entitled to full wages with wages from 1st December, 1948, when the strike took place. Held further, also that the stoppage of work for about 2 to 4 hours in the circumstances of this case was not an illegal strike.

The appellant, a film producer, was granted a certificate of film under section 5A of the . The certificate was certified by the Central Board of Film Censors. The certificate issued to the appellant was not conclusive evidence of any corrupt practice committed by him in relation to the exhibition of films. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the central Board of film Censor and finding in favour of the appellant, the film having been duly certified for public exhibition, the public exhibition was circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The High court has rightly dismissed the writ petition. [5A B] (1) Section 79 of the Penal Code is general and after having elaborately enacted such a legislation can it be that a certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 292 I.P.C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the certificate of the Board of Censure has been granted by the competent authority, may constitute an offence and bona fide belief, although mistaken, litigates or is justified by law in doing it. [ 517 E F] (2) The High Courts have rightly dismissed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [511 G H] (3) The certificate granted by expert authori ty can be dissociated from the certificate issued under section 79 of I. P.C.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate General for the Patna District, in the Patna High Court. He was also a member of the Bar Council of Bihar. The petitioner challenged his appointment by filing a writ petition before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucrative services, and that his clients are entitled to seek lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high office of Government Pleader bylaning him as a battery of lawyers. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner 's client ' was not a legally protected party in the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that his case is covered by Article 14 of the Constitu tion and that the Government Pleader had no right to seek anything more than what he had already done. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Constitution (Forty Second Amendment) Act, 1978 does not confer any power on the Supreme Court to issue a writ of mandamus or direction in respect of any matter which is directly and substantially in issue in a foreign court. [760C] 2.1 Article 14 forbids class legislation but does not forbid reasonable classification for purposes of legislation. The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and it cannot be said that there is any differentia which has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. [764D E] 2:2 In order to find out whether Government Pleader is a legally covered party, the Court must consider the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the people who are the third world clients, and practice internal distributive justice oriented on basic social justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling to the star of material amassment immunised by law from the liabilities of other occupations. [774E F] 2 :3 The Court must examine the quality or service control the prices, floorto ceiling, enforcement commitment to people who were the third country clients and practice inside the Secretariat or outside the State. [754G H] 2 .2 In a case where there are several thousand cases in the High Courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals, it is but right that Government should sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf for the sake of material Amassment to calculate income on a speculative basis. [758C D] 2 2.3 The Government Pleader and in a sense, every member of his legal profession has a higher dedication to the public.

The appellants held shares of the Bank of India in a public limited company. The shares were purchased by the Bank and the right to apply for the shares was reserved among the shareholders. The appellants filed applications under section 66(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, claiming that they had been holding shares on the date of the application. The Income tax Officer rejected the applications. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the transfer by the Mills to the Bank was not a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of that Act and that the shares were not liable to be distributed among the members of the company. In further appeals to the Tribunal, the High Court held that since the shares had been offered by the appellants to their shareholders, they could not be regarded as dividend within section 2 (6A). The High Court also rejected the contention that the distribution of the right was a distribution within the extended meaning of that expression in section 2. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was wrong in holding that the distributed by the mills amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the definition of section2(6 A) and that, therefore, the distribution must be deemed to have been dividend within that meaning. HELD: (i) The expression "dispute" is not defined in the Act. It is a term of wide import and includes all disputes arising out of or relating to such matters as are capable of being resolved by arbitration. [587 C] (ii) The definition of "cividend", in section 3(6) of Income Tax, 1922 is an inclusive one and not an exhaustive definition. The definition does not purport to distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividend. It did not also take the form of a resolution for distribution of dividends. [588 E] (iii) The word "daccumulated" in section 12(6B) of Act, is not an inclusive and not a mere expression of wide amplitude. The word 'dividends ' has been defined in section 4(1) to mean any share holder or share holder of a company which is a public company. [589 F] (iv) The High court erred in holding the distribution as dividend by the appellant on the basis that the share holders were holding shares at the time when the application for the issue of the shares, was made. The High Courts had not taken into account both the normal and the extended definition of dividend. [592 G] (v) The words "different shares" in the definition are wide enough to include shares which have a monetary value. But by the form Of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the resolution could not he altered.

The appellant was declared elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant on various grounds including the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the respondent had failed to prove that the witnesses who were kept present in the court were not examined and that the names of the witnesses were not mentioned in the list filed under sub rule (1) and that they were not produced in compliance with order XVI Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub section (1), of Section 87 of the Act is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the court is t necessary. If mere omission to mention the name of a witness in the List envisaged by sub rule(1), and who can be produced without the assistance, it was not necessary to provide in Rule 1A that the party may bring any witness to give evidence or to produce documents without applying for summons under R. 1. [532C D] 2. The requirement of sub rule 1A is that the parties must have sufficient cause for the omission to specify the name and address of a particular witness. If a person who has not been examined in Court on the date fixed for recording his evidence, fails to do so, Rule 1 A of order XVI would not have omitted to mention that only those witnesses kept present could be examined whose names are mentioned in sub rule 2. [540D E] 3. The failure to mention these names in the lists contemplated by sub section(1)(a) and (b) of Section 88 of the 1951 Act, is in regard to witnesses to whom the party would produce before the Court without the aid of the Court. If it was implicit in Rule IA that it only enables the party to examine only those persons whose names were mentioned in list envisaged by Sub rule (2), the party could do so under Rule 1B of order XVIII. [541E F] 4. The omission to state the name or names of a person not shown in the Lists contemplated by Sub Rule (1)(b) and who could be produced before the court without the help of the High Court, is an error apparent on the face of the record.

The appellant was appointed Principal of a College in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He was appointed as Principal of the college on May 1, 1981. The order of appointment stated that the Committee of Management had no power to make any appointment and therefore the Committee had no authority to make the appointment. The appellant challenged the validity of the order by means of writ petition before the High Court which held that the order contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing powers of appointment of Principal and teachers. The High Court held that there was no power of appointment as Principal, and therefore, the Committee was not competent to make appointment. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the date on which appellant was made Principal was irrelevant because the date of his appointment was not relevant for the purpose of determining whether he was appointed or not; that the Selection Committee had the power to appoint the appellant and the appointment of the Principal was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment was otherwise valid, though ineffective and if it was valid and power to made appointment was withdrawn or suspended it would not be open to the Selection Commit tee to make and select appellant nor the Manager on behalf Of the Committee could issue appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant. [982C] 2. The Committee of management had no right to select the appellant nor did it have any power to direct the Committee to make appointments. If the power was not suspended it was open to it to make an order modifying or rescinding the regulation or making any other order consistent with the provisions of the Act, the second contention of the respondent that the appointment was illegal and therefore invalid cannot be sustained. [8982F] 3. The word 'appointment ' in section 9 does not mean merely a transfer but also a transfer from one person to another. It is only when the appointment is made by an order under section 9 that it can be said that the power of the Committee has been withdrawn or revoked. If it was intended to operate retrospectively, then it could have no effect on the validity or otherwise of the appointment and if the power had not been exercised, it would have been open to a Selection Committee to pass any consequential order. [9082F G] 4. The power to grant approval is conferred by the regulations. It has been conferred on the State Govern ment without making any reference to the Board to make its own rules consistent with law and the Act. The Rules do not confer any power on the Government to make a recommendation for appointment. If there was any such power, it could be said to have been exercised in an arbitrary manner. [9182G H] 5. The State Government could be deemed to have rescinded that power under section 10 of the , if the order was valid. But as there was nothing on record to show that the Government had any power or authority to cancel the appointment, it was not open to them to contend that the Board had no such power. [9282A] 6. The fact that the appellant was a member of the College in which he was working would not make him ineligible for appointment and hence his appointment could be made only by a body not authorised to make such appointment and cannot be challenged on the ground that the authority has no power or jurisdiction to make it. [9382C D] 7. The Government had no powers to make appoint ment. If any person has been appointed as Head of an Institution in contravention of the provisions contained in the Act he is bound to suffer for the same. But if the action was taken by the State, the appellant would be entitled to recover any salary paid to him. [9482F H] 8. The question whether the appointment made was illegal or not has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case.

The Delhi Cloth Mills Ltd. was a manufacturer of tyres to whom the fabric was supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The petitioners, who were manufacturers of tyres, challenged the validity of the order of assessment on the ground that the goods called "rayon tyre cord fabric" sold by them were not "end product" within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Delhi Cloth Mill that the High Court should have interfered with the matter in favour of the appellant. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts should not decide whether the "tyre cord fabric ' is an exempted "fabric" or not. [503C] (2) The word "textiles" has been used in the Oxford Dictionary to mean "a textile". It means "any kind of cloth". Therefore, unless there is a clear cut distinction between "yarn" and "woven fabric", it cannot be said that the word "feel" is not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sell their own product which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption. [500D E] (3) The words "textile" and 'woven fabrics" have been used interchangeably with the words "yimmingate the cloth". The word 'fabric ' has been defined in the Act to mean any kind of fabric which is a textile. It does not, therefore, appear that there was any error apparent on the face of the record. [525E F] (4) The expression "tool" is used in a sense in contradistinction to "woollen fabrics". Therefore the word 'textiles ' has to be understood in its popular sense as meaning "any type of cloth." [501F G] (5) The use of the word `yarn ' in the context in which it occurs shows that it is meant for "totton" fabrics and not for any kind or fabric. Therefore, even if the tyres are parts of a fabric, they have to be regarded as an item of fabric. [506F G; 506A] (6) The fact that the tyres manufactured by the petitioners were not in a fabric which was capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar Textiles fabric does not make any difference.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal from the mines and also doing allied and incidental work. The respondent workman was residing at Dhanbad, while he was residing there. On account of his residence at Dhanbad he was staying at Dhanbad. He was residing near a railway station, Dhanbad. In the year 1988, the management transferred him to Dhanbad. The appellant company filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33 B of the for transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view to the difficulties expressed by him to attend the labour court, Dhanbad and transferring the proceeding to the Labour court, Patna. The Labour Court passed an order on August 8, 1988 transferring the case from the LabourCourt, Dhanbad to Labour Court, Patna for speedy disposal. The management transferred the proceeding from the labour Court, Dhanbad, to Labour court Patna. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of section 33B of the Act, the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the workman and without opportunity to the management, transferred the case to Labour Courts, Patna, for speedy trial. The Management transferred the proceedings from the Court of Labour Court Dhanbad to the labour courts, Patna on August 9, 1988. The petitioner company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the transfer order contending that the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workmen and transferring him to the State Bank of India was not competent to transfer the case as he had been residing at Hajipur and it would be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour courts, Bihar. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Govern ment before accepting his representa tions and transferring them from Dhanbad to Patna should have given an opportunity to both parties to lead evidence in support of their respective cases. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that the transfer of the case was a transfer from one Income Tax Officer within the State to another without any notice to the workman, and that the order transferring the proceedings to the High court was bad as the Government had not given an opportu nity to the Management to lead any evidence in its support. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The transfer of a case from one Incometax Officer within State to an Income Tax officer without it except of course where the very object of the transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected and he is afforded a reasonable opportunity of representing his views on the question and the reasons of the order are reduced accordingly. [297C] 1.2 The Government was misled by the representation of the respondent workman. He has not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition, and not seriously disputed the factum of his residen tial residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad and he has been residing there with him. It is true that in the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the management it was stated that the respondent had no concern with the residence of the petitioner company at Dhanbad but it was denied by the management that the petitioner had transferred the matter from Dhanbad. [298F] 1:3. The Government has not given any opportunity to all parties to adduce evidence in this regard. It has also not denied that the documents referred to in the Special leave petition, and the counter affidavits filed by the respondent are seriously disputed.

The appellant, a hotel establishment, was the management of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The dispute between the parties related to the payment of wages to the workmen employed in the hotel. The management referred the dispute to the Additional Industrial Tribunal, Delhi, under section 10(1) of the , for adjudication. The reference was made by the Government of India under section 12 (4) of that Act. The appellant contended that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it; one was that the union could not be made a party to the reference, and the other was that there was no dispute between them. Held, that the dispute was not one relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen. The words "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union" in section 10 (1) were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workman should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. The fact that in the order of reference the words " as represented by a hotel Workers ' union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " have been added did not affect the competence of the order. The word "as representing" in the context means "to represent the workmen". The word 'as representing ' is used to denote the existence of an industrial dispute between employers and employees. The expression "as represents by the hotel Workers" has been defined in section 2 (k) of Act as meaning "any dispute or difference between employers, employees and employees". The words 'as represented ' are not confined to disputes between employers 'and employees but include disputes between workmen and their employers. The definition of "industrial dispute" is wide enough to cover all industrial disputes which are connected with the employment or non employment or terms of service of the employees. It does not include disputes relating to conditions of employment, nor do they include disputes regarding the payment or termination of employment of any person. The question whether a particular dispute is one relating only to conditions or conditions or labour of an employer depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms and conditions of reference. The mere fact that the parties to the dispute are clearly specified, namely, (1 ) the management which is the management, of the hotel, and (2) its workmen, does not affect their jurisdiction to refer a dispute for adjudication under the ,.

The appellant imported a total duty of Rs.2,87,690/ . The Customs authorities assessed the goods under Heading No. 84.06 and also imposed a penalty of Rs, 1,00,000/ on the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal before the Collector of Customs (Appeals) which was dismissed by the Customs Excise and Gold Control Appellate Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the words "parts thereof" in Heading No 84.07 refer to internal combustion piston engines, but not to the parts of internal combustionpiston engine, and that even assuming that the bushes and bearings are not identical articles but they are distinct and separate, yet there is no material for holding that the highways which have been imported by the appellant are parts of the engines referred to in Heading Nos. 8406.06. The Customs Authorities should embark upon the question and decide whether the bushes, which have already been imported, are parts or not. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The Notification does not refer to the part of internal bore pistons but only refers to the other parts of such engines. [84F] 1.2. The notification is applicable to parts of engines mentioned under Heading 84.05. [85G] 1:3. The words "internal combustion pistson engines" are not defined in the Notification. They have been used in the sense of a number of other types of engines, and they are not intended to be used for the purpose of the exemption granted by the Notification, irrespective of the fact that they or any of them have already undergone the operation of the notification. [86G] 2.1 The Notification is applicable only to parts which are part of the engine, but it also mentions the parts thereof. So, although the parts are not mentioned under heading No.84.06, by necessary implication and in the context of the Notification the word "part" has been used. [87H; 87A] 2:2. In view of the finding that the Notification exempts also parts of a engines, as mentioned under Entry No. 83.06 of Heading No., it is necessary that the Customs authorities should embark on the question, and decide, whether the highways imported by them are really parts of those engines.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration of their title to the offerings in the Dargah and also for possession of the offerings made by them. The defendants pleaded that they were not entitled to any right of Mujawar as the right was given only to the male members and not to the females. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove ouster of Fathima Bee from the right or claim of any share in the offerings. The first appellate court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the second appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that the rights of Fatima Bee had become barred by limitation by exclusion of Fathi Bee 's title at the time of the judgment of the High court in 1909 and another ground taken was that neither Fathita Bee nor the plaintiffs were entitled to claim any right or interest in the management or offerings in their offerings. In the second appeals, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the defendants had not been able to prove that Fathula Bee ever made a demand or asked for a share of the Hundial collections as such it should be held that her rights had become extinct and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathila Bee were also not entitled. On behalf of respondents it was submitted that the High Courts were right in holding that they had failed in establishing ouster of the right of FATHima Bee or the plaintiffs, and that the appellants had failed miserably to prove their ouster from the fight or management of the Dargah. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High courts were right when they held that rights of the Fathuma Bee had became barred by exclusion. [526C] 1.2 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathite Bee or plaintiffs, it must be shown that there was a clear intention on the part of the defendants to exclude Fathina Bee from their right or share in any offerings.

The appellant, a contractor, was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The respondent 's claim for house rent was rejected by the Authority on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from his wages. The Authority held that the house rent allowances claimed were admissible in respect of the house and that the appellant was not liable to pay house rent. On appeal, the Appellate Authority allowed the appeal holding that the House rent allowance was not a "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the terms of the contract between the parties included rule 3(i) and therefore the position in law is that there is no absolute right in the 1st respondent to claim the house allowance; (ii) the House Rent Allowance which was payable to every employee of a particular category but the rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. HELD : (i)(a) The rules which must be included in the terms Of contract between parties, contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceases to be so entitled, whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. But it has been argued on behalf Of the 1 st respondent that rule 3 (i), which provides that the employee should be posted at a place where he has no other suitable type of accommodation, must create absolute right and an employee cannot claim any house allowance in respect thereof. [174 B C] (b) The Rules do not contemplate the grant of house rent to every employees of a specified category but only the rules which are applicable to them. Rule 3(1) does not make it obligatory on the employer to allot the accommodation to the employee who has refused to vacate the accommodation so offered to the servant.

The detenu was detained under section 3(1) of the (for short, called 'the Act '). The grounds of detention were served on him. He challenged his detention by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of detention was void because the concerned Minister of State Government never passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166(3) of Constitution, the detenu could not be deprived of his right to make a representation against his detention. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the detenus, mechanically refused to supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated March 14, 1980 which in fact was received by the detenu on March 25, 1980. [352B] 2. The supply of the earlier statements which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been with held, could not by any reckoning, expose those persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partisans of the detenu. There was thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of grounds of the detention, all the basic material relied upon or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make an effective representation at the earliest. [353C D] 3. The right to have a representation is not absolute and unfettered but is subject to the limitations imposed by Article 22(5) of our Constitution. It is open to any person aggrieved by the detention to prefer an appeal against his order, if he so desires, to challenge the legality or validity of the order on the ground that the grounds are vague or irrelevant. [351D E] 4. The detenu has a right to be heard before the order is made and it is not open to him to contend that the detention was mala fide. It was on this short ground that he had acquired the gems in question from those persons. There is thus an infringement of the Constitutional imperative that the detenu should have been afforded the earliest opportunity to make his representation against the order. [354E] 5. The delay of more than a month, in supplying the copies to the detenus has vitiated the detention. It must be borne in mind that the right to representation is a fundamental right and it cannot be denied that it is an absolute right. [355F G] 6. The representation made by the petitioner was not considered by the detaining authority as expeditiously as possible. There were no grounds for making any such representation. The detention order was therefore void because it affected the detenu 's right to represent against his illegal detention. [356G H] 7. The fact that the representation was rejected on March 14 and the rejection of the request by the Collector, without applying the mind to its nature, is a circumstance which cannot be taken into consideration at all. [359B C] 8. The order of the Governor dated April 23, had allowed the writ petitions and directed the release of the detained. It did not make any reference to the earlier orders of detention. There Was no mention in the grounds of such orders that the petitioner had been informed about his right of making a representation. [360C D]. 9. The State Government was not bound by the order passed by the Central Government on April 23. The only question for consideration was whether the order was vitiated because the relevant documents were not supplied to him. There could be no doubt that the supply was made in good faith and in good interest. It would be a matter of great deal of care and attention. [361D E]. 10. The grounds on which the detention order had been passed, were entirely different from those on which it was based.

The appellant was convicted by the trial court under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the joint appeal by several accused persons jointly tried and acquitted by the Sessions Judge was incompetent as the joint appeals were not maintainable under section 419 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. HELD: (1) The High court was wrong in holding that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal. [647 D] (2) The word "appeal" in section 419 means an appeal in a case, and not against an accused person who has been acquitted. Section 419 does not in terms cover the case of an appeal by the State against several accused person jointly tried. [643 F G] (3) The question whether a joint appeals by several persons convicted at one trial must be upheld or not is a matter to be decided on the basis that the earlier decision is wrong itself giving effect to that view. If one Division Bench of a High Court is unable to distinguish a previous decision of another Division Bench and holding the view that the later decision is erroneous, it is difficult to negative the maintainability. [641 F G; 642 A] (4) The Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High Court rightly distinguished and explained this decision.

The assessee was a firm carrying on business in foreign territory. The income tax authorities held that the income from house properties owned by the assessee was not liable to tax under the 1918 Act but only receipt of income in British India and as such the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 had no application. The High Court held that in the case of business carried on in foreign territories the business as such is not liable under the provisions of the 1918 act but only receipts from the profits of the foreign business and there was no tax on the foreign income. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the assessee being a resident in India, he could not be said to have been charged under the 1922 Act because the income received by him was derived from the foreign firm and was in relation to it and it must therefore be taken that there was an assessment to tax on foreign business within the meaning of section 25(3) of the 1922. Act. HELD: (i) The assessee was entitled to relief under section 25 (3) in respect of interest on securities as well as for income from other sources. [912 D] (ii) The High Courts have taken the view that the foreign company was not charged under section 3 of the Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the appellant from the Indian business and not the foreign profits. [936 G H] (iii) The question whether the foreign agency of the assessee is liable to pay tax in respect Of interest on security or income arises only when the income is paid to the foreign partner.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the appellant. The appellant was to supply the bricks in accordance with the agreed rates. At the instance of the assessee the Tribunal referred the question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a works contract and not a works contracts. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not an agreement for sale. [163E] 2. The question whether the transaction contemplated by the Contract entered into between the applicant and the public works Department of Government of the State of Gujarat was a work contract or a works contractor depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [164F] 3. The nature of the contract is not decisive, but it is justified by the principal terms governing the contract to which we will presently refer. [165G] 4. The fact that the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondent for the construction of the Capital Project in question was not decisive. [166H] 5. The contractor could not sell the bricks to third parties without previous permission of the company. In Chandra Bhan Gosain 's case (supra) dealing with those very common features this Court observed as follows: "Clause 3 of the Contract in that case though prima facie word cd as regards the relevant clauses in similar fashion as the contract in the instant case is in fact cast in a different mould and it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the said contract that the decision of the purchaser in Chandra Bhanj Gosain`s case was a sale and cannot be regarded as a works con tract. [167H; 168A] 6. The Court is not right in answering the question against the assessee. [168B] 7. The judgment of the High court in Chandra Mohan Gosain vs State of U.P., (supra), dealing with the same question, was not correct. [169F] 8. The agreement entered into on September6, 1965 was a contract for sale and the supply of bricks after manufacture. It is true that the contractor could sell his contract without such permission but this was not a case where the contract was in fact executed by him. [170E] Chandra Bhanja Gosain & Co. vs State Of U. P., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, who was a member of the Lok Sabha and elected to the Rajya Sabha in March, 1971, filed an application before the President of India under Article 32 of the Constitution for a direction that the Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd December, 1971 by the President be revoked by the Vice President acting as the President by virtue of his powers under sub clause (b) of clause (4) of Article 352 of the Constitu tion. The petitioner contended that the period of five years (being the period for which the House of People may, under clause (2) of article 83 of the constitution, continue from the date appointed for its first meeting) in relation to the present House of the People should be extended for a period not exceeding one year at a time. The President acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers, by his order dated 27th March, 1977, revoked the Proclamation and the proclamation of Emergency dated 25th June 1975 issued under clause 4 of Article 356 of the Consti tution. The Petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation on the ground that the duration of the House was not fixed for a term of five year at which the President had ceased to be in operation on 3 12 1971, and since the two Proclamations of Emergency were not published in the official Gazette, they could not be considered as having been issued in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the petition. Dismissing the Petition, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the property in dispute was private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the authorities. The trial court held that the premises were not private property but were private properties and therefore the appellant could not claim any right or title to the said property. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court and found that the suit was not maintainable as the judgment of the High court had been set aside by the High 'Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that the properties were private property, and that the appeal did not involve any substantial question of law. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding the property as a public temple. [156 B] (ii) The question whether the property was a private or a public Temple could have been decided by the trial Court only on the basis of the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property is the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the trial Judge was not right in assuming that whether the properties are private or public temple, it was incapable of valuation. [157 C] (iii) The suit was filed by the appellant in the form of an application under Order 1,126, 6 0, in the first instance and was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the Court. It was therefore not open to the High. Court to have proceeded on the assumption that whether property is a private one or a private temple.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant. The appellant 's claim was rejected by the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffing of its employees. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffins to its employees, and that the company was bound to pay the same to them in that behalf. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The appellant has throughout been making provision for tiffering retirement benefits on the basis of the settlement arrived at between the parties. [573 D] (ii) The Tribunal had overlooked the fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations and the appellant cannot, therefore, be blamed on that account; but there are some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. [574 E F] (iii) The fact that a worker has been paid wages for t he work done by him does not make any difference because the workers have been paid the same wages as they were employed by the employer. [575 G H] (iv) The question whether the appellant is under an obligations to provide certain cash allowance or not was essentially one of fact and it could not be said that the Tribunal had ignored the fact.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Bank of India. He applied for transfer of his provident fund account from one bank to another and deposited in the Reserve Bank ofIndia the amount due on his behalf. The Union of India, however, did not pay the amount. The respondent thereupon filed a suit against the Union of indus trial court for recovery of the amount as arrears of land revenue. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the money represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was not "illegal" and without jurisdiction. HELD: (i) The respondent was entitled to immunity from attachment. The order of attachment was therefore in excess of the powers conferred on the Bank by section 50 of the Indian Contract Act. [1413 D] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that the amount in the hands of the Reserve bank of India had ceased to be provident fund property money and was liable to be attached. [1513 E F] (iii) The Union Government was a trustee for the subscriber of the money. When the amount lying with the Reserve is attached, the Union has clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal of attachment. [1614 G] (iv) The Bank was in respect of the provident fund moneys in the position of a trustee and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and to remit it to Browne. The Reserve Bank was, as already stated, the agent of the Railway Administration for conversion of the amounts into sterling. [1714 G H] (v) The Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1947, which came into force on January 1, 1948, provided that "where under this Act any payment is to be made to a subscriber in sterling, the amount shall be deemed to have been paid out to him". The Bank had also an interest in the provident Fund account. When it was required by the Reserve Government to send the amount by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the bankers of Browne at Birmingham, the money remained at the disposal of the Bank as provident fund and was exempt from attachment [1715 G H; 1716 A] (vi) The State Bank was a Trustee for the subscribers of the moneys. When a cheque was converted into rupees in sterling it was not the agent or the Reserve Manager of the railway administration for conversion to sterling and was not its agent. The Bank could not be said to have acted as an agent of Birme at the time when the amount became due to him.

The appellant was a pump manufacturing enterprise, issuing a notice to the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 33 of the , before the Labour Court for reinstatement in service with full back wages and allowances. The Labour Court held that the termination was not bona fide but was a colourable exercise of power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Labour court and directed reinstatement with full backwages. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the finding of fact recorded by the Labour Appellate Tribunal was not perverse; (ii) the respondent had no opportunity to meet the charge; and (iii) the termination of service was mala fide. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the order terminating the services was not a camouflage or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. [497 F] (2) The respondent had not been able to show that the action regarded as punitive it was bad, there having been no enquiry whatsoever with liberty to the employee to meet his charge. [498 A B] (3) The termination of services was a camouflage and amounted to victimisation or an unfair labour practices. If it came to the conclusion that the respondent was a cleanly minded person undesirable, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. [500 C D] (4) The power of the Court to go behind the language of the order is reiterated there.

The petitioners, who were the victims of a tragedy, filed a Writ Petition in the High Court praying for directions to the State Government to initiate appropriate action against those responsible for the tragedy. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Court should not interfere with the right of the victims for damages on the footing that the persons who organised the 'eye camp ' were acting pursuant to and under the authority of Government and that on the doctrine of State action the activity must be reckoned as that of the State itself which must, accordingly, be held vicariously liable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The factual foundation laid before the Court and the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine o f State action. [245C] 1.2 In the course of his counter affidavit, the respondents have stated that they had been paid a sum of Rs.5,000 by way of interim relief. The petitioners have not denied that this was a wholly avoidable mishap and is entirely the result of the composite negligence on the part of the surgical team and the authorities of the U.P. State Government. [246D] 1:3. In view of the findings of the High Courts, the factual foundation for the proceedings No appeal could he made to this Court to the decree of the doctrine. [243E F] 1 :4. The factual foundations laid before this Court and limited scope for the proceeding no appeal can be made tO the doctrine as it stands today. [244F G] 1 Whether or not the State should approach the matters not with spirit of law but would depend on the proceedings, as a matter of course, must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [242G H] 2.1 In the instant case, the averments made in the writ petition and the counter affidavit are absolutely silent about the norms for conduct and management of eye camps. The guidelines laid down by the Government in that behalf have been updated and revised. The recommendations of the expert sub committee of the Indian Medical Council may be consid ered by the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.2.1988. [239H; 240A] 2:2. On humanitarian consideration, the victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the State Govern ment.

The Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984 was enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Assam. Section 3(1)(c) of the said Act provides that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asom Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commencement of the Ordinance by a Notification dated 15th December, 1984. The petitioners who were members of the Board of Directors of the Asoms Committee and the Executive Council of the State Government challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that it was violative of Article 19(1) (c) and was also violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act and the noti fication issued under section 3 were ultra vires by which a Board was nominated to replace the Karyapalika and byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalikka. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act and its provisions are not violative of any constitutional provision. [164G] 1.2 The Act is an Act to provide for temporary transfer of management and control of affairs of a AsomRBPU.

The appellant was married to Kamala Devi on May 10, 1938. The marriage was performed in December, 1938 and the gift was made at Deoghar. On May 10 , 1940, the appellant made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of her daughter as she had no male issue. The gift was confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which was really a part of the marriage ceremony while the gift in question was made some two years after the marriage. On June 30, 1940, a deed of gift was executed by the appellant in favour Of Kamala Devi and the deed of gifts was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1940. The respondents contended that the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband to her daughter subsequent to the marriage, the gift made long after the marriages ceremony was for or at the time of the execution and registration of the deed. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the relief which she claimed. The deed of gifted in favour was not a valid gift within the meaning of section 14(1) of the Hindu Law as it was not made at the date of the gift but only confirmed on March 11, 1940 and registered. The question whether a gift is of reasonable or religious nature must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. Held further, that in view of the provisions of section 15 of the Indian Contract Act, the plaintiffs respondents were not entitled under the law to the reliefs which they claimed.

The first respondent, a voter in the constituency of the District Faridkot, was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged his election by an election petition on the ground that he had committed corrupt practices under section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice were clearly proved and that the appellant had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the poster in question was a printed pamphlet and circulated by the first respondent and therefore, the appellant was not guilty of any corrupt practice as contemplated by section 123 (2) Of the Act; (ii) the allegation of corrupt practices were clearly established. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The allegations of the corrupt practices alleged are clearly proved. [416D] 2. The allegation of bribery is clearly established and there was no evidence to prove that the poster was circulated by a person who had been authorised to do so by the candidate or his agent. It is also clear from the evidence that the first appellant was known to him. He was not even aware of the contents of the poster. [417E] 3. The poster said to have been printed and circulated are Annexures P 1 and P 2 which appear at page 42 of the second paper book and it may be necessary to extract certain portions thereof "Keeping in view the present conditions in the country it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. [414F] 4. The evidence of the first appel lant shows that a few (viz.) the appellant, who was the only candidate for the election, had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the posters by Tej Singh had been clearly admitted by him, as indicated above. [413D E] 5. In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the appellant cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [411E F] 6. The effect of the hoarding of the hoardings by Tej. Singh has been clearly established by him. [409F] 7. In the circumstances, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh was actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing. [420G H] 8. The result is that the appeal is allowed and the election of the respondent (Tej. Singh) is set aside.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was appointed as a Forest Secretary to the Government of Punjab. The Chief Minister of the State was requested to take up the matter with the Chief Minister. The appellant filed an application for contempt against Shri Bhajanlal alleging that he had committed contempt of court and that he was guilty of criminal contempt. The Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the High Courts exercising their jurisdiction under Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt, are only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor; and that the jurisdiction to punish for contempt is not available under section 19(1) of the Act only against any decision or order of a High Court passed in exercise of its jurisdiction to impose a punishment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court exercises its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 when it imposed a punishment of contempt. [893G] 2.1 The High Courts have jurisdiction to punishing for contempt including also the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to punish a person for contempt. It does not mean that when the High court erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of Criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without remedy. [889H; 890A] 2:2 The jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitu tion is to punish an offender for contempt of itself. It is for the first time that under section 20(1), a right of appeal has been provided for. After furnishing such information he may still assist the court, but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only three parties, viz., the Court, and the contempt pro ceeder. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right of Appeal on the petitioner for contempt and acquits him, such decision of the high court acquitting the contemnor is made in the exercise of the jurisdiction under article 215 of Constitution. [881B C] 2 :3 The High courts exercising their jurisdic tion or power to punish the petitioner under Article 216 of the Consti tution are only one party, namely the Court. It cannot be said that when a court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in a particular manner, the exercise or power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other.

The appellant was the owner of certain agricultural lands in Bombay. The rent note showed that the land had been leased to the respondent for a period of 10 years and the lease was for a term of 10 year. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment on the ground that he had failed to pay the rent within the prescribed time. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in second appeal held that the provisions of section 111(g) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 were applicable to the case and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provision in sub section (g) Of section III of the Act was not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience and could not govern leases made prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases executed prior to 1st April, 1930. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the suit was maintainable against the respondent. The provisions of sub section(g), (g), and (h) of section III were intended to protect tenants from eviction on the grounds of default in payment of rent, and as such the provisions contained in sub s.(g) were not applicable to leases granted prior to January 1, 1930, and could be enforced.

The appellant, a workman, was dismissed from service by the Management on the ground that he had been found guilty of misconduct. The Labour Court held that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to him before inflicting the punishment. The High Court confirmed the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Arbitrator had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan; (ii) the High Court had confirmed the view of the Tribunal that the second opportunity being given to a workman after conclusion of the inquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting on him the punishment of dismissal, the punishment was not vitiated by not affording him an opportunity to offer any explanation; and (iii) the interference with the penalty of dismissal in respect of Rama Shanker and Baramapradan was erroneous while another writ petition filed by the management was allowed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The second part of the Standing Order deals with several punishments and requires finding of guilt in respect thereof. [367E] 2.1 The High Courts have confirmed the conclusion of fact reached by the Arbitrator that the first part of Standing Order dealing with several punishment and requiring finding of guilty in respect to each one of them and this procedure is different from that which has been contemplated in the last part of it. [368F G] 2(a) The second clause of the sub section deals with two distinct stages concerning disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to show cause has been provided for. But the plain reading of the said Standing Order read as a whole does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, it is not possible to sustain the construction placed on Standing Order No. 17. [369F G; 370A] 2 (b) The only ground on which the inquiry was held to be invalid by the arbitrator and by the High court must disappear. The solitary ground onwhich the inquiry has been held to he invalid having disappeared it must follow that the Arbitrator has no jurisdiction to enter into merits of the case or interfere with punishment of dismissing inflicted upon Rama Shankar, and Burma Pradhan.

The Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 was amended by Act 35 of 1969. Section 7D of the Act provides that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1957 shall be deemed to be tenants if he or his predecessor in interest occupied such land knowing it to be the property of the Government. The Kerala Land Reform (Amendment) Act, 1969 was passed by the State Legislature and the Kerala Land Tribunal (Amendment and Validation) Act 1970 was passed. Section 6D of this Act provides for a declaration that any person occupying land under lease granted before the commencement of the Kerala Estates Abolition Act, 1964 shall be liable to pay compensation at the rate of one per cent of the amount of rent payable by him in respect of such land. The appellant tenant filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the amendment and the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) Section 7 D of the 1963 Act was not applicable as amended by Kerala Land Revenue (Amendment & Validation) Bill, 1968 which was introduced in the Kerala Legislature by the Kerala Amendment Act 35/ 1969; (ii) Section 6B of the Land Reforms (Amendment Act 1970 which provided for a summary determination of compensation payable to a person occupying any land on the basis of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed granted by a competent person to be deemed tenants, was invalid and such land had been in continuous occupation of such person for not more than ten y years immediately before the 11 th day of 4th April,1957; (iii) Section 5A of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1970 which provides for summary determination is ultra vires the Kerala Revenue Tribunal (Second Amendment) Act. 1970 and the Validation Act is void as it offends Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the amendment made by the Amending Act 35 / 1969 was valid. [112D] 2. Section 4(1)(a) of the Madras Land Reforms and Resumption of Ceiling on Land Act, 1961 is not applicable to a case where the tenant occupying land has been in occupation of the land of another situate in his occupation for more than 10 years immediately prior to 11th April 1957. [113E] 3. Section 5 A of the 1971 Act provides a summary remedy to a tenant if he has paid or tendered rent within a period of ten years from the 11st day of the last day of that year, on the ground that the land is not required for his personal cultivation. The proviso to section 7D(1) provides that where any person in occupation has been continuously in occupation as a tenant for more then ten years before the 1st day Of April 1957, such period shall be calculated from the date of such occupation and the amount paid or payable by such person shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue. [114F G] 4. Section 8D(2) provides for an appeal against the order of eviction passed under section 6 of the 1970 Act to the District Judge who has delivered a judgment or decree in the suit filed before him. The expression "any other person" occurring in the said provision is not defined in the Act. [115G] 5. Section 9D(3) provides a special procedure for summary eviction of tenants from land held by them on the strength of an agreement, which may be executed between the landlord and the tenant.

The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the . The prosecution alleged that the goods were smuggled into India without an import licence and in contravention of the provisions of the Import & Export (Control) Act, 1947. The appellant denied having been in possession of the offending goods but stated that he had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove that the articles in question were smuggled goods and that the appellant was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. On appeal, the High Court held that the evidence of the appellant did not establish that he knew that the portion in which the boxes were kept was in appellant 's exclusive possession with all that was contained in it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The onus of proving that the article in question was smuggled goods lies on the person from whose possession the goods are seized. [541 G] (2) The burden of proving the fact that the said articles were actually smuggled or brought into India is on the prosecution. It is not necessary for the prosecution to prove the fact as to who had brought those articles. In the present case, the appellant had not produced evidence to prove his possession at all. [542 B] (3) The appellant had failed in proving that he was dealing in them knowing they to be illegally imported or smuggled. He had not led any evidence that the sub tenants were placed there. There is no evidence which could enable the appellant to know where the goods came from or when the goods, were imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them.

The appellants were the President of a Association which was registered under the Madhya Pradesh Societies Registration Act, 1935. The members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of yarn and yarn. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for accounts of the profits and yarn on the ground that the Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Act. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1934, are mandatory in character and do not contravene article 14 of the Constitution. The object of the Act is to provide for the acquisition by the company of gain and to make provision for the distribution of profits among its members at a fair price. The Act does not contemplate that the company should be registered as an unregistered firm. It is only when it is registered that the registration can be granted that the provisions of the section apply. The scheme of the , shows that the object of a registered firm is to carry on business which has for its objects the acquisition or sale of gain, and not to enter into any contract with regard to the profits of the business. The fact that the members of a Registered Association are not registered would not make them liable to be registered under section 4 of the Indian Companies Act.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 5(2)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0.1986 they along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1 of the compartment No 1 of a train. On 8. 6. 1986 at about 2.00 P.M., they alongwith two others were travelling in a car driven by one of the respondents. The car was stopped by the driver and the driver. The respondents were arrested on 8th June, 1986 and taken into custody. The police filed charge sheet against the three respondents under section 120B read with Section 420 I.P.C. and section 5 (2)(a) readwith section 5 of the Act. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the respondents on the ground that an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police. On appeal, the Judicial Magistrate held that the charge sheet was not maintainable because the two offences were substantially "the same offence" as Section 120B I. P.C., and quashed the proceedings against the respondents and ordered issuance of process against them. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by the respondents holding that the two charges framed against the two respondents were not maintainable and that the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of an offence and ordering issue of summons to the accused. Hence this appeal by special leave.
