Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The test is whether taking the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Court will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under Section 482 of the Code. [463E] 1.2 In the instant case, the ingredients of an offense under section 499 I.p.C are not part of the offences under sections 500 and 501 I.PC. The ingredients of the said offence are not parts of the same as Section Nariman that the specific allegation in the present case concerns the specific act of killing of an elephants, ald that such an offence at all events, falls within the overlapping areas between of section 42 I.A.C.; and therefore constitutes the same offences apart from the fact that this is a distinct offence under section 42, IPC. [465F G] 1:3. The test for determining whether cognizance of any offence against the act, relevant to the matter, has been taken into consideration by the High Courts in regard to the first ground, obviously, does not serve to support the order of the High court in the instant cases. [467B C] 2.1 In the present cases, prima facie, the ingredient of an alleged offence under Section 9(i) read alongwith 50(l) of I.T. Act is the same or substantially the same. The tests are: (a) taking the allegation and the complainant as they have been, without add or sub tracting anything; if no offences are made out, then the Court will not be justified under Section 50(1). [467C D] 2:2. In the circumstances of the case, there is no scope for interference with the order passed by the trial court in Crl. No. 259/1987(R) 18.2.1987. [468D] 3. The question whether cognizance has been or not taken and whether the complaint has been filed on the basis of a charge sheet does not in law constitute an offence under the IPC and at the same time constitutes an abuse of the process of the court or not. [470E F] 4.

The petitioner was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of rigorous imprisonment for a period of two years. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) the law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges, and (2) the courts have no power to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law in this case is that the accused should ordinarily be released on bail by the court to further the ends of justice and nothing in Sec. 389(1) which reads: 389 (1): Pending any appeal by a convicted person the Appellate Court may for reasons to be recorded by it in writing, order that the execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and also if he is in confinement, that he be released from custody on bail or on his own bond. [343G H] 2. The vice of the system is brought out in the Report: "the evil of bail is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. " [344H; 344A B] 3. A liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own bond, with or without sureties. [344C D] 4. The practice which is now being followed in the United States is that bail covers both release on a single bond, but not a heavy punishment and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [345D E] 5. An accused in judicial custody, actual or potential, may be released by the Court to further, the ends Of justice and anything in Sec tion 389( 1) which read with sec. 389 (2), is the reach of the law, not the money tag. The best guarantee of presence in court is the reaching of the Law, notthe money tag but the power of the court. [346F G] 6. An under trial is worse of than a convict or that the powerof the court cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. It cannot be that an accused in a judicial custody when the conviction is for reasons which are poor and weaker sections of the community to get equal justice under law. And, if he has one, and is deprived of an opportunity to work out his sentence, he can safely release the accused on his personal bond without bail. [347G H; 347A B C] 7. The courts have power to refuse bail to a surety when the guilt is established. The discretion of the Court in granting bail is not the same as that of the High Court. It is only the court which has the power to grant bail and it cannot be said that an under trial was worse of the accused. [349B C] 8. An order rejecting a surety for a sum of Rs. 2,000 or Rs. 3,000 on his behalf without sureties will stultify the sub section; for then, an accused is released on his bond without surety. [350C D].

The assessee, a registered firm, had at different places in India branches one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity 'Eldee '. The business carried on by Eldees ' Castle Mills was that of a registered partnership firm. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of six years from the income of Eastle 's business as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle `. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had not been included in the assessment of the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assess ment in question of the income from 'Cantle '. In further appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the findings of the Appellate Tribunal were one of facts and not conclusive. [434 C] The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal is based on no evidence except the inference drawn from the circumstances found by it. It must be shown that the Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at its conclusion. If the conclusion of the Income Tax Officer was based upon some evidence ignoring other relevant matters, it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the incomes of 'Centle ' in the income by the Incometax Officer may have been a relevant circumstance but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner relied.

The Minister concerned in the writ petition filed by V.P. Duggal respondent challenged the order fixing seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The respondent filed an appeal against that order before the High Court which directed that the Minister concerned be impleaded as a party in the petition. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the Secretary concerned was not a necessary or proper party. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that since the Minister had been called upon to file his personal affidavit, he should have filed an affidavit. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The direction for impleading of the Minister as a respondent in the Writ Petition is set aside and the Minister is directed to file an affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the amended petition. [972C] 2. The order fixing the seniority of engineers n tho Irrigation Department was passed on November 18, 1974 that the minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties. It is essentially for the Minister dealing with the matter and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. [963D] 3. The directions for impleading the Minister are set aside. [952E] 4. The Secretary concerned should file his affidavit. [941F] 5. The Chief Minister should file an affidavits. It may be open to him to decide in the light of the allegations contained in the earlier petition as to whether he should or should not file an afflux of those allegations, if he so deemed proper.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of rent and other payments under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in revision reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the view taken by the High court that arrears of rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section259 of the Act is incorrect. Held: (i) Section 259 of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1913, does not confer any power on the Board to recover rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the section. The provisions of section 259 are intended to protect the interests of the general public and it is only when the rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Act or the rules made thereunder that the Board may require any occupier of such property or of any part thereof to pay to it, instead of to the owner. The words "any tax" in section 259 do not mean that the provisions of the section are intended for recovery only if such rent is recovered by a board or a military Estates Officer. (ii)The words "other payments" in the Act refer only to rent directly claimable under the statute and not to a suit or a summary proceeding as provided in the Section. The word "rent" in this context means "any sum due by a committee under this Act". Therefore, the provisions in section 260 of the Indian Income tax Act can be utilised for realisation of arrears of land revenue on land and buildings only if the rent in the sate is recoverable from the owner under section 256 and it further provides that any amount recovered from any occupier instead of from an owner under sub section (1) shall, in the absence of any contract between the owner and the occupier to the contrary, be deemed to have been paid to the person entitled to receive the rent.

The appellant was in the service of the respondent company as a Section Salesman. The respondent company terminated his services on 12th July, 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The appellant challenged the termination order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent Company had been appointed as a section salesman for certain number of districts and in the area of each section salesmen and local travelling salesmen were appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination of the services of the appel lant by the respondent was illegal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of this enactment and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Disputes Act. [474G] 1.2. In order to come within section 2(s) of the Industrial Dispute Act, as it stood in 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated, the employee has to be 'under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature. The finding of the Labour Court on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. [473A B] 1:3. In the instant case, the appellant was employed to do canvassing and promote sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study Of the market condition. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. [476C D] 1 :4. In view of the finding that the is not applicable to him and in view of his fact that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage.

The respondent Company was a company registered under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007. The Company was in possession of land in question at any time prior to the coming into force of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950. The company had been paying rent agreed upon between the Government and the Company prior to its grant of the lease. The State Government issued a Notification under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue & Tenancy Act 1950 declaring that the land in dispute was held by the Company as a tenant under the State Government. The respondent Company filed an application before the Additional Collector for eviction of the Company on the ground that the Company had been holding the land for a period of more than three years prior to 1.10.1977 and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. The Additional Collector held that the company was not a 'pakka ' tenant within the meaning of section 181 of the Code and that the respondent Company had failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the tenancy. The appeal filed by the company before the Collector was dismissed. The High Court confirmed the order of the Additional Collec tor. In the Special Leave Petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State was not an 'pagka ' within the definition of section 185 of the code and that, therefore the Company could not be evicted by summary proceedings provided for under that section. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "pakki" in section 181 means a person who holds land from the State Govern ment or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by the State. [179F] 2.1 Section 182 of the Cr. P.C. provides that where any person holds land under the Government, he shall be called a 'Pakka". The expression 'pakhki ' has been defined in section 185(2) of M. P., Land Revenue Act, 1901 to mean a person holding land from a State Government or to which a right is granted under the Code. [180F] 3.1 The word 'pankka ' has not been defined either in the Code or in the Madhya Pra desh Adhiniyam, 1950, but in the M P. Land revenue and Tenancy Acts, Sambads, Mahalas, Alienating Lands) Rules, 1951, which were the law in force until repealed by the M .P. Abolition of proprietary rights (Estate, Mahal and Alienated Land) Act 1950. [181F G] 3(a) The word "pakhk" has been used in the sense of a person 's own land ' and not as a mere name or name. It is not and cannot be disputed that the original lease was obtained from the predecessor State and the company continued to remain in possession thereof under the newly stipulated terms agreed upon by the parties to enable the Company to remain In possession of the land as a lessee. [182B C] 3.(b) The expression `pakk ' has to be read ejusdem generis with the word `pakhka '. It cannot be said that the word 'Pakhk ' is used in contradistinction to `pankki ' or `paggi '. [183C D] 4. In view of the provisions of section 183 of the Act, the Company has been at all material times a Government lessee in respect of the lands in question.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for compulsory acquisition of land in an estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The Act was amended by the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment) Act 15 of 1965 which provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part, on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. Section 1(3) of the principal Act provides that where any law does not provide for the transfer of the ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the state, it "shall not be deemed to provide, for the compulsory acquisition or requisitioning of property, notwithstanding that it deprives any person of his property. The appellant who was a member of the Orissa Legislative Assembly and whose land was acquired under the Act, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 47 of the Land Reforms (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1965 which provides for compensation not based on the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 47 was inconsistent with article 31 A of the Constitution and was void as it contravened article 14 of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 1 (3) is not a law in force when the United State was formed. It is only when the land is within tho ceiling limit that section 1( 3) can be said to have been enacted. [357E] (2) The Act is not extended by a notification under section 1 (1)(3).

The widow of her husband 's estate had, in fact, no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversionary heir. The widow died leaving behind two sons, namely, the appellant and the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that the widow had no interest in the property and that the appellant had no right to claim any share therein. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The widow 's right to challenge the right of a prior alienee from the widow is not a limited interest of her own at all and, therefore, could not be surrendered to the reversioner. [355 D] (ii) The rule that a surrender by a Hindu widow of his property without any legal necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse possession against her is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. [356 F] (iii) The position of a person who has acquired by adverse Possession the limited interest in his property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as the widow remains alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of the widow which no doubt benefits the reversioner in the sense that he gets the inheritance even during the widow ' s lifetime. [358 F] In the present case, the widow was under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. The reversionary right to question it is no part of her estate at all. [359 B C] (iv) The reversional right to challenged in a suit is no separate property and cannot be surrendered by a stranger who has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on his expectation of enjoyment by the reversioner, which no question of fraud or collusion that might arise, is not available to the reversioners. [360 F G] (v) The fact that the reversioner does not derive his title from her will is immaterial because she does not acquire any title from the husband or his spiritual benefit against her.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Uttar Pradesh. The Cotton Mills Company was formed on March 1, 1956 and it had been running a textile mill for the manufacture of cotton yarn. In the year 1957 the Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., which was a public limited company, was declared an insolvent by the High Court of Allahabad. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of Rs. 10 lakhs from the respondent on the ground that the shares in question had been pledged with the Government of Uttar pradesh and that the sale proceeds thereof were not sufficient to discharge the debts due to the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to join as a requisitionist of a meeting under section 169 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 and that he had failed to comply with the provisions of the Act. The High Court also held that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member under section 170 of the Income Tax Act readwith section 190 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the special notice under section 284(2) and (5) of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertaking (Dies Recovery) Rules, 1958 issued by the Collector of Kanpur in exercise of his powers under section 149 of the Indian Income Tax Acts were invalid as they contravened the provisions contained in sections 172 to 178 A of the said Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment of the shares of the Polytex Company held by the Cotton Mill Company had not deprived the holder of the share whose name is entered in the Register of Members of the company the right to vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under Section 169 of Act. [878C] 2.1 The attachment was made with a view to protect the interests of the shareholders and to prevent the holding of the meeting of the Company or to give effect to the provisions thereof. It is not necessary that the order should be passed in the nature of a charge under section 168 of the I.T. Act read along with section 190(1)(a) of U. P. Government Electricity Supply Act, 1948. [888C D] 2:2 The attachment and sale of the goods in question were not made by the appellant in exercise or purported to be exercised under section 17AA (1)(b) of that Act. It was not necessary for the appellant to have obtained any order from the Collector under section 18AA (I) (a) or (5). [889D E] 2 :3 The attachment had been made with the object of protecting the interests and interest of the respondent company. The sale proceeds were to be deposited in the Government Treasury. The amount was to be paid within a period of six months from the date of the order. The Collector could not, therefore, be said to have acted mala fide or in violation of any provision of law.

The petitioners, who were owners of a house in the State of Punjab, filed a suit for declaration that they were owners in possession of the land along with some others. The Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The Gram Panchayat in its written statement inter alia pleaded that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 and therefore the suit was not maintainable. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the question involved in the suit being merely one of title to the suit land and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit property was shamlat deh or not, the suit could not be maintained by virtue Of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court which held that since in the case involved in a suit was merely one such of title, it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Panchayat that the court before which a suit had instituted had not framed any issue as required under section 13A of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation). Act 1961 and consequently the suit filed against the Panchayat was not competent. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the trial court had jurisdiction in the matter. [833C] 2. The plaintiff in the instant case had not claimed a declaration that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat or that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. It was therefore, not possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamilat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under Act or in respect of any matter which the Commission or the Gram panchayat is empowered by or under the provisions of the . [834E F] 3. The suit had not be filed against Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the suit lands belonged to them as shamillat deh. It will not be possible in this case for the Civil Court to make any declaration in respect thereof without deciding whether the land was shamat deh or otherwise. [884G] 4. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration of that property. They have, however, claimed that they had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Land Revenue Act and not by the Civil court. [894A] 5. The civil court has jurisdiction to decide such claims in such manner as may be prescribed. [90G] 6. In the instant cases, the Panchayat which had been impleaded was raising the plea that the plaintiffs were owners along with others of the suit house.
